#5616. 12 housing bills that could shape affordability after the midterms

Concerns over housing supply and affordability have reached a fever pitch and become a major issue for voters in this year’s midterms.

With the midterm elections just days away, housing affordability remains a pressing issue for voters — and a growing legislative priority for lawmakers in Washington.

Congress has spent much of the past two years considering proposals aimed at lowering housing costs, helping first-time buyers, unlocking existing inventory and encouraging new construction. But despite growing bipartisan interest in housing policy, many of those proposals remain stalled in committee as voters prepare to decide which party will control Congress.

Lawmakers scored a significant bipartisan victory in July with the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a sweeping package aimed at boosting housing supply and addressing barriers to development. Yet much of the broader housing agenda remains unfinished, including proposals to expand homebuyer assistance, increase affordable housing investment and raise the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Some bills have continued attracting additional congressional support in recent weeks, but none of the proposals highlighted in September has advanced since. With both chambers largely out of session until after Election Day on Nov. 3, further legislative action will likely have to wait until lawmakers return to Washington.

Inman revisited the most consequential housing bills that could help shape the federal government’s approach to supply, affordability and homeownership in the next Congress.

What it does: The bipartisan legislation would double the capital gains exclusion on the sale of a primary residence, from $250,000 to $500,000 for individuals and from $500,000 to $1 million for married couples, and automatically adjust those limits over time to account for inflation. Why it matters: Supporters argue that the limits, which have remained unchanged since 1997, discourage longtime owners with substantial equity from selling and effectively lock inventory off the market. NAR has made the proposal a major 2026 priority and is currently framing it as one of the fastest ways to increase existing-home supply. Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means and the Senate bill before Finance, and neither has advanced beyond referral. Support has continued growing, however, with 159 House cosponsors and 25 Senate cosponsors as of late October, including lawmakers from both parties. With Congress largely out of session until after the election, inclusion in a broader tax package during the lame-duck session or next Congress remains one possible path forward.

What it does: This legislation would establish a refundable federal tax credit equal to 10 percent of a first home’s purchase price, capped at $15,000. Eligibility and the size of the credit would be subject to income and local home-price limits.

Why it matters: Unlike proposals intended to increase supply over time, the bill would directly reduce the cost of purchasing a first home for qualifying households. The tradeoff is that giving buyers more purchasing power does not add more homes to the market, and in a supply-constrained market, it can also put upward pressure on prices.

Status: Both versions were introduced in July 2025 and remain before the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees, respectively. Neither chamber has taken action beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., the bill would increase the mandatory share of Federal Home Loan Bank earnings devoted to the system’s Affordable Housing Program. The Consumer Federation of America estimates the change would generate roughly $300 million in additional annual funding for affordable housing development, down payment assistance and home repair programs, without requiring additional taxpayer funding.

Why it matters: The 11 Federal Home Loan Banks provide liquidity to more than 6,500 member institutions, including banks, credit unions and community development financial institutions. Housing advocates have argued that the system should devote more of its earnings to its public mission. In a broader reform proposal, the Coalition for Federal Home Loan Bank Reform has called for doubling the mandatory Affordable Housing Program contribution from 10 percent to 20 percent, which it estimates would add about $600 million annually for affordable housing.

Status: The House Financial Services Committee considered H.R. 10325 on Sept. 16, but a motion to report the amended bill favorably failed 21–28. That leaves the measure facing a significant setback in the House, even as housing and consumer groups continue pushing for broader FHLBank reform.

What it does: Designed to make it easier to pull together a down payment, this bill would raise the amount first-time buyers can withdraw from an IRA without paying the usual 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty from $10,000 to $50,000.

Why it matters: The proposal targets a major barrier for many prospective first-time buyers: saving enough cash for a home’s down payment and covering closing costs. It would expand access to buyers’ existing retirement savings rather than create a new federal subsidy. NAR lists the bill among its current legislative priorities.

Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate companion, introduced by Sens. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., and Todd Young, R-Ind., is before Finance. Neither has advanced beyond committee, though the Senate bill’s bipartisan sponsorship distinguishes it from some other first-time buyer proposals.

What it does: Seeking to make homebuilding and rehabilitation more feasible in distressed neighborhoods, this legislation would create a federal tax credit to support the construction and rehabilitation of owner-occupied homes where development costs exceed what finished properties can command on the market. The credit is designed to help close that gap and make projects financially viable.

Why it matters: The credit is intended to make starter-home projects possible in communities where builders currently cannot make the numbers work, with a particular focus on for-sale housing rather than rental development.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance. In May, the bipartisan sponsors released planned revisions, including more flexibility for state housing finance agencies and a shorter four-year authorization, that they intend to carry into the next version of the bill, whether in a year-end package or the next Congress.

What it does: This proposal would establish a federal investment tax credit covering 20 percent of qualifying costs to convert nonresidential buildings into housing, increasing to 30 percent in certain areas where development is particularly challenging. At least 20 percent of the resulting units would need to remain affordable to households earning no more than 80 percent of area median income for 30 years.

Why it matters: The bill targets two persistent real estate problems at once — underutilized commercial buildings and the shortage of housing. Office-to-residential conversions have attracted substantial interest, but challenging layouts, financing hurdles and construction costs can make projects difficult to pencil out. A tax credit is intended to help close that feasibility gap. NAR also lists this bill among its 2026 legislative priorities.

Status: Introduced in March 2025, the bipartisan bill has attracted 57 cosponsors, including lawmakers from both parties, but remains before the House Ways and Means Committee without advancing beyond referral.

What it does: Focused on expanding and modernizing the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, the proposal includes a broad series of changes involving tenant eligibility, project financing and credit administration.

Why it matters: LIHTC is a central federal financing tool that helps drive the construction of affordable rental housing across the country. Congress already adopted two pieces of the broader proposal in 2025, permanently increasing annual Housing Credit authority by 12 percent and lowering the bond-financing threshold from 50 percent to 25 percent. According to the National Council of State Housing Agencies, roughly two dozen other provisions remain unenacted.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance, with both measures drawing broad bipartisan support. Advocates continue pushing the remaining provisions either through the standalone bills or as part of future tax legislation.

What it does: The bill would update federal rules for mortgage revenue bonds and mortgage credit certificates used by state housing finance agencies, including increasing limits on certain home improvement loans and changing refinancing and recapture provisions.

Why it matters: Those programs can help lower- and moderate-income households access lower-cost mortgage financing, giving this technical tax legislation a direct connection to homeownership affordability.

Status: The House version, introduced in February 2026, remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate bill remains before Finance. The Senate measure was discussed during an Oct. 21, 2025, Senate Banking housing subcommittee hearing, but neither version has advanced beyond committee.

What it does: Seeking to open underused land owned by churches and other religious organizations to new housing development, this bill would preempt certain state and local laws that block affordable housing on those properties.

Why it matters: Religious institutions collectively control substantial amounts of land, including parcels in expensive housing markets where zoning can constrain redevelopment. The bill is notable because it tackles supply by asserting federal authority over certain local land-use restrictions, rather than relying primarily on grants or tax incentives.

Status: Introduced by Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., and Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., in September 2025, the bipartisan legislation remains before the House Financial Services Committee. Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes, D-Ohio, joined as a cosponsor in October, but the bill has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: This measure would amend the Fair Housing Act to prohibit discrimination based on a person’s source of income, veteran status or military status.

Why it matters: The change would expand federal fair-housing protections for veterans, service members and renters who rely on housing vouchers or other lawful sources of income. It could also create new federal compliance obligations for landlords, property managers and real estate professionals.

Status: Both versions remain in committee, with the House bill before Judiciary and the Senate measure before Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs. The House proposal has continued attracting support, reaching 23 cosponsors following the addition of Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, on Oct. 22. Neither chamber has advanced the legislation beyond referral.

What it does: Rather than establishing a tax credit or housing-production program, the Saving the American Dream Act would require HUD, Treasury, Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and the Federal Housing Finance Agency to coordinate housing research and market data and submit a joint report to Congress identifying opportunities to improve housing affordability.

Why it matters: Federal housing policy is currently divided among HUD, Treasury and other agencies. Supporters of the effort argue that greater coordination could reduce conflicting policies and give Washington a more coherent strategy for addressing affordability.

Status: Introduced in September 2025, the bipartisan bill remains before the House Financial Services Committee and the Veterans’ Affairs Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity. It has attracted 40 cosponsors, including two who joined on Oct. 1, but has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Norma Torres, D-Calif., on Oct. 22, the legislation would establish a new HUD grant program to help states streamline financing and administrative processes for affordable housing development. The proposal would authorize $90 million annually from fiscal 2027 through 2029, including funding to consolidate state financing programs, simplify applications for builders and improve access to development assistance.

Why it matters: Affordable housing developers often navigate multiple state agencies, financing programs and administrative requirements to move projects forward. By simplifying those processes, the proposal aims to reduce administrative barriers that can delay projects and increase development costs. States that meet the bill’s initial requirements could also use funding to streamline zoning, permitting and Low-Income Housing Tax Credit administration.

Status: Torres introduced the bill without cosponsors on Oct. 22, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee. It has not advanced beyond committee referral.

NAR’s current legislative agenda is centered heavily on housing supply, with the trade group estimating the country is short 4.7 million homes. Following the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July, NAR has continued pressing lawmakers on housing supply, with its latest advocacy materials putting particular emphasis on unlocking existing inventory through the More Homes on the Market Act and proposed changes to the capital gains exclusion for longtime homeowners.

The organization is also pushing lawmakers to fully fund several HUD programs, including fair housing enforcement and housing counseling services, while calling for long-term reauthorization of the National Flood Insurance Program. NAR says the flood program supports roughly 500,000 home sales each year and argues that lapses or uncertainty around coverage can disrupt transactions in flood-prone communities.

The flood insurance program’s current authorization expires Dec. 11, the same day a temporary spending measure funding federal agencies, including HUD, is set to expire. The deadlines leave Congress facing another round of funding and insurance negotiations during its post-election lame-duck session.

Passage of ROAD has not ended NAR’s work on the legislation itself. Many of the law’s new grants and housing programs still depend on future congressional appropriations and HUD rulemaking, including incentives for local housing production, zoning and permitting reforms, commercial-to-residential conversions and home-repair programs. NAR is now encouraging states and local governments to prepare for those programs, while pressing Congress to provide the funding needed to put them into effect.

Implementation of the law is also underway. On Oct. 22, the Treasury Department proposed regulations clarifying restrictions on large institutional investors purchasing single-family homes. Under the law, beginning Jan. 7, 2027, investors controlling at least 350 single-family homes will generally be prohibited from purchasing additional properties, subject to exceptions for activities including build-to-rent and renovate-to-rent programs.

For qualifying programs designed to help renters become homeowners, the proposal also establishes a framework for a 30-day first-look period and a right of first refusal before investors sell the properties to other buyers.

Reporter’s note: This story was originally published on Sept. 24, 2026, and has been updated to reflect the latest available information.

Additional note: AI tools were utilized in reviewing and verifying current federal housing bills, legislative priorities and related reporting for this story. All substantive details were checked against congressional records, primary-source materials and prior reporting before publication.

#5615. Oracle connects AI-driven testing with a new approach to database security

Frontier AI models that uncover software flaws by the hundreds are forcing database providers into larger, faster patch cycles, and real application testing is becoming the safeguard that keeps those fixes from breaking production systems. The same AI wave is also undermining security rules written into applications.

Oracle Corp. has responded on two fronts, hardening its code against outside attackers while moving agent controls down to the data layer. The first effort began when the company turned an early-access frontier model on its own software, according to Juan Loaiza (pictured), executive vice president of Oracle Database Technologies at Oracle.

“Back in March, we got early access to the Mythos model and we ran it against our code and it started finding all these security vulnerabilities,” Loaiza said. “It’s turning up some very serious security issues. And so we said, ‘Hey, this is a code red moment. The house is on fire.'”

Loaiza spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why AI-discovered vulnerabilities, AI-generated code and AI agents require enterprises to treat security as a data problem. (* Disclosure below.)

Most of Oracle’s response to AI-discovered vulnerabilities is landing in its regular quarterly patches, which have grown much larger as a result, Loaiza explained. Customers must automate patching and stay current, but every large patch raises fears of regression in systems that cannot fail.

“We have something called Real Application Testing where we can capture real workload and run it to make sure that your workload is not affected by these patches,” Loaiza said. “It’s not quite as simple as just apply because the applications that people run are extraordinarily complex. They run entire countries, entire industries.”

Patching handles outside attackers. Internal AI use is a separate threat, because applications have traditionally enforced end-user security, and AI now writes much of that code or goes straight to the data. Oracle’s answer is Deep Data Security, which began shipping in April and passes an authenticated user’s identity as an encrypted token through to the database. The company has since extended those authorization controls across remote databases, lakehouse data and related tables.

“The new world as I see it is all these end-user security rules have to be enforced where AI can’t bypass them, which means all the way down in the data,” Loaiza said. “The AI agent has to get your identity. It’s acting on behalf of you. It can’t leak the data if it can’t see the data.”

Business rules follow the same logic. Application code has always blocked a credit card charge above the customer’s limit, but an AI agent told to enforce that rule may not comply, Loaiza noted. Oracle is providing declarative ways to define such rules, along with SQL Assertions that check whether changes made through SQL are valid.

“There’s credit limits, there’s all sorts of things that are business rules that can’t be violated. And again, if we move those all the way down into the data, then no matter how you access the data, what mechanism you use, how AI is used, it cannot violate those rules,” Loaiza said.

#5614. Bitcoin Price Slides, Washington’s Political Balance Shifts, Trump’s Crypto Agenda at Risk

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price fell toward $75,700 as Democrats captured the Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, raising fresh uncertainty over Trump’s crypto agenda. But Bitcoin has now recovered to $77,700 during Asian trading hours, but remained under pressure as Nasdaq futures plunged and investors reassessed Washington’s political balance.

Democrats secured control of the Senate in a sweeping rebuke to President Donald Trump, winning key races in Texas, Ohio, North Carolina, Kansas and South Carolina. The House outcome remained closely contested, with Democrats also making significant gains.

The result threatens to complicate Trump’s push for clearer crypto regulations. Bitcoin price weakness now reflects both market risk aversion and concerns that Congress could delay legislation designed to establish a federal framework for digital assets.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitcoin briefly dropped more than $2,000 after early election results pointed toward a Democratic victory, falling from nearly $78,000 to the $75,000 level. Buyers subsequently stepped in, lifting BTC toward $77,700 this morning.

The selloff extended beyond crypto markets. Nasdaq 100 futures dropped as much as 2.3%, while S&P 500 futures fell 1.3% as investors reacted to the possibility of tighter oversight of technology companies and AI infrastructure projects.

BREAKING: The S&P 500 is now on track to open below 7,500 for the first time since July 31st as markets price-in a Democrat victory in both the House and Senate.Nasdaq 100 futures are now down more than -2% tonight. pic.twitter.com/mBbq77a2mG

The dollar also weakened, while the 10-year Treasury yield slipped six basis points to around 4.90%. The moves raised concerns that a Democratic-controlled Congress could limit Trump’s tax and spending agenda, while increasing regulatory scrutiny across several industries.

Bitcoin’s decline followed an already difficult period for digital assets. The king had slipped below $77,000 earlier in the week as technology stocks weakened and investors reduced exposure to riskier assets.

The election adds another source of uncertainty, although Bitcoin’s recovery from its overnight low shows people have not fully abandoned the market.

The biggest crypto-specific concern involves the Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act, which aims to establish clearer rules governing digital assets and divide oversight responsibilities between U.S. regulators.

The legislation failed to advance through a Senate procedural vote in September, falling short of the 60 votes required. Democrats opposed the measure over concerns about ethics provisions and Trump’s crypto-related business interests.

A Democratic-controlled Senate could make the bill’s path more difficult, particularly if lawmakers prioritize stronger safeguards and additional oversight of the crypto industry.

The election also gives Democrats greater power to investigate the administration and examine potential conflicts of interest involving Trump’s digital asset ventures. Congressional scrutiny could intensify even without new legislation.

However, the result does not automatically mean crypto regulation will become more restrictive. Democrats have supported regulatory frameworks for digital assets, but disagree with Republicans over enforcement, consumer protections and safeguards against political conflicts.

The immediate risk is that negotiations become slower and more complicated, leaving crypto firms without the regulatory clarity they have sought.

Bitcoin price direction will likely depend on whether the election-driven selloff spreads into a deeper market correction. A sustained recovery in Nasdaq could help Bitcoin regain momentum, particularly if investors begin treating the election result as a temporary source of uncertainty rather than a lasting threat to risk assets.

On the other hand, continued weakness in technology stocks could pressure BTC and altcoins further. Investors will also watch whether Democrats pursue aggressive investigations or push for substantial changes to crypto legislation.

The political shift could create a more difficult environment for Trump’s crypto agenda during the final two years of his presidency. Yet a divided government may also limit sweeping policy changes from either party.

For now, Bitcoin price remains caught between broader market weakness and uncertainty over U.S. crypto regulation. The election has changed the political landscape, but the next moves in Congress will determine whether the impact becomes a lasting obstacle for the industry.

#5613. Carson Daly Has a New ‘Today’ Gig—Inside the Sprawling Long Island Estate He Calls Home When He’s Not in the Studio

Carson Daly’s weekends just got a whole lot busier—the “Today” host will join the Saturday edition of the show as a co-anchor.

The TV personality shared the news on the Nov. 5 episode of “Today,” noting that he’ll be joining existing co-anchor Laura Jarrett while upholding his weekday broadcast duties.

According to NBC News, Carson, 53, had been working as the interim “Saturday Today” anchor since September.

“I should just say, I’ve been very lucky to have a lot of TV gigs, but this one’s really special,” he said on the show. “At my age and at my stage of my career, to have an opportunity to come in and sit next to Laura and to learn and to get better at my job and be the best broadcaster that I can, it’s not something I take lightly.”

Nov. 7 will be Carson’s first official day as co-anchor.

“We’re going to have a lot of fun on Saturday,” he said. “But most importantly, the best part about the gig, like here during the week—which I’ll still be here during the week—is getting to go to your place of employment with such high-quality human beings. We are a family, and the fact that I get to spend one more day in this building, six days a week, is an absolute honor.”

When Carson isn’t spending time at the New York City studios that “Today” is filmed in, he has a beautiful family home in Manhasset, NY.

In 2013, the “Total Request Live” alum snapped up a six-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom estate for $6.5 million, according to The Sun. Carson purchased the home—which is about 25 miles northeast of Manhattan—for $6.5 million.

The Colonial-style abode is a gorgeous escape from the bustle of the city and includes a pool and a pool house.

Carson shared a glimpse inside the home in 2020, when he posted a snapshot of his family celebrating Easter. He noted that he was “especially grateful” for his family’s “blessings,” as he and his wife, Siri Daly, and their four young children virtually participated in their Catholic parish’s services next to a cozy fire in the living room.

“The Voice” host also shared some personal details about his sleeping arrangements with his wife, revealing they had a “sleep divorce” that was the “best thing that happened” to their marriage.

While his wife was expecting the couple’s fourth child in November 2019, Carson told “Today” viewers why the pair choose to seek out separate beds.

“I have sleep apnea, my wife’s pregnant, and during a home renovation, we downgraded to a queen-size bed. We just felt like we’re better off sleeping in different beds,” he said.

He joked that his CPAP machine makes a shared bed feel “like sleeping next to Darth Vader.”

“Most women would want to sleep in another bedroom,” he said. “I don’t snore anymore, but the noise of the machine keeps her up.”

In 2022, Carson confirmed that the arrangement continued after the baby was born.

“We both, admittedly, slept better apart,” he said on the “Today” show in 2022.

Siri is also part of the “Today” crew, where she works as a regular food contributor.

On social media, the chef and cookbook author often shares content from the family’s gorgeous kitchen, which has loads of cabinet space, sprawling counters, a subway tile backsplash, and even a “baking nook.”

In November 2023, Siri posted about her love of crafting intricate holiday tablescapes, joking that “no one is allowed to eat and mess it up,” while showing the tastefully decorated dining room.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5612. Open Real Estate: We’re almost there, but not quite

OPINION: The Open Real Estate options give sellers just two choices: market or participant view. Darryl Davis makes the case for a third door.

Picture a homeowner at the kitchen table. She likes you. She trusts you. And she says something agents hear every week: “I want you to sell my house. Just you. I don’t want a parade of strangers walking through my bedroom with agents I have never met. But I don’t want to hide it either. Advertise it. Get the word out. I want the best price.”

That is not a strange request. Some homeowners would happily give up a few dollars on the sale price for less stress, more convenience, and the peace of working with one agent and one office. And right now, the newest system in real estate has no way to say yes to it.

On October 26, Keller Williams, AGNT (the parent of eXp and NextHome), HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group launched Open Real Estate (ORE). Four competitors came together to stop listings from disappearing into company silos. They deserve real credit. But read the FAQ, and you will see the system gives a seller only two doors.

Now go back to our homeowner. Door one sends strangers through her bedroom. Door two gives her one agent but forbids anyone to advertise her house, the last thing she asked for. She wants one agent and full marketing. ORE makes her pick one.

That is not seller choice. That is a choice between two things she did not ask for.

Here is the option that is missing, and it is simple.

I can already hear the objection. “Darryl, isn’t this just a pocket listing with a nicer name?”

No. A pocket listing is hidden. A Coming Soon tease builds buzz while keeping other agents out, and nobody, not even the listing agent, can show it. The true exclusive is the opposite of both. The house is actively marketed to the public, and every member company knows it is available. The only thing exclusive is who walks through her front door.

Think of a restaurant that only takes reservations. Everybody sees the menu and knows where it is. You call first, and the owner decides who gets a table. Nobody calls that a secret restaurant.

Let’s say it out loud. In a true exclusive, the listing agent may well sell the house to their own buyer and get paid on both sides. For some sellers, that is exactly why they choose it. They understand that one cook in the kitchen managing the whole process beats two, especially when the second one is an untrained buyer’s agent.

ORE already has what it needs to offer this, and technology can make the fiduciary piece stronger than ever.

CCP had the right intentions. NAR wanted to stop listings from disappearing. But it was the wrong strategy, and it did the opposite. Once a listing is publicly marketed, it must go into the MLS within one business day.

Keep it quiet, though, and it falls under the office exclusive exemption. That does not tell agents to share. It tells them to stop advertising and keep the listing inside their own company. The brokerage itself became the pocket.

A rule meant to bring listings into the open pushed many further underground. As I wrote earlier this year, a Redfin analysis found pocket listings rose 67 percent after CCP passed. NAR leaves enforcement to local MLSs, and in a lot of markets, they have quietly stopped enforcing it or issuing penalties. A rule on the books but not enforced protects no one. It only confuses the agents trying to follow it.

For newer agents: Before CCP, a seller could hire one brokerage to market and show her home exclusively. But those exclusives usually stayed out of the MLS, so other agents often never knew the house existed. The true exclusive keeps what sellers liked about the old way and adds what was always missing: every agent knowing the house is for sale. That is the replacement.

Let’s give our homeowner the third door: one agent, full marketing and a way for the right buyer to find her. That is real seller choice.

Until a model like this is in place, we are still hurting buyers and sellers. Period.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Darryl Davis is the CEO of Darryl Davis Seminars. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5611. Research prediction: Shift from digital banking to AI-driven finance will transform financial services in 2027

The coming year will signal an abrupt transition from digital banking to intelligent finance, as AI agents and operating models reshape the ways that financial firms acquire customers and provide advice.

This is the central thesis of a new Forrester Research report, “Predictions 2027: Banking and Investing.” The findings were summarized from data involving 915 respondents in the U.S., U.K., and Canada.

Forrester identified several key points of transition. These included fundamental changes through automation in financial discovery and guidance journeys, as well as a belief that although one-third of banks will announce an AI transformation program, only 5% will succeed.

“In 2027, financial services will enter a new phase in which intelligence becomes the primary source of value creation,” said Forrester researchers in the report. “AI assistants are reshaping how customers discover, evaluate and act on financial products; investment participation is expanding despite persistent economic anxiety; and banks are racing to determine whether AI will merely enhance existing operations or fundamentally transform them.”

Forrester’s prediction of a 5% success rate is based on a belief that many banks will rebrand existing AI initiatives as AI-native without significant changes in operational infrastructure. Retention of legacy processes and operating models will prevent an ability to scale AI deployment, a fundamental requirement that AI technology providers such as Dell Technologies Inc. are emphasizing to their clients in the financial services world.

“Ultimately, I think we’ve enough proof points now that AI works and it works really well and it gives you speed and efficiency in your company,” according to David Kennedy, chief financial officer of Dell, during a recent interview with theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. “The question is, can you do that at scale?”

One way that financial institutions will pursue scale is through mergers and acquisitions. Forrester predicts that AI banking technology M&A will increase by 50% in 2027. Acquisition of proprietary data assets, governance capabilities, and AI-native orchestration will require an ability to navigate hybrid computing environments, a need that compute providers such as Advanced Micro Devices Inc. has seen among its own customers.

“As a provider of AI compute, we want to make sure that we are enabling those enterprises to not only run their AI tasks through the frontier APIs in the cloud, but we are providing them infrastructure that they can host open-weight models very efficiently on-prem,” said Suresh Andani, corporate vice president of compute and enterprise AI at AMD, in an interview with theCUBE. “Every enterprise conversation I’m in, that’s a key topic of discussion.”

Another key topic involves AI agents and their growing influence in the enterprise. According to Forrester’s findings, 40% of banks will launch AI assistants next year. The challenge for many financial institutions will be leveraging AI assistants to deliver differentiated guidance using proprietary data, decisioning and specialist expertise to guide customers. This is where keeping proprietary knowledge in-house can become a distinct advantage, according to John Roese, global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell.

“It doesn’t mean you can’t use frontier models and open models,” Roese told theCUBE. “It just means that when you design your AI system, you need to realize that the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools. It’s not even the models. It’s the special knowledge that’s now manifesting in these new forms that really captured what you know and do differently than your competitors.”

#5610. Active Inventory Grows as Sellers Keep Homes on the Market

As the holiday season approaches, housing market activity on both the buyer and seller sides are cooling right along with the temperatures. Moving toward what is typically a slower time for the housing market anyway, a new report shows buyers are holding back as elevated rates continue to diminish their buying power and sellers are bringing fewer homes to market, but not broadly delisting.

According to the Realtor.com’s  October monthly housing report, new listings fell 7.5% year over year, the steepest decline of 2026, while 4.4% of active listings were delisted, compared with 4.6% a year earlier. The preliminary share of listings with price cuts was 20.5%, just 0.2 percentage points above last year and down from September.

Meanwhile, the report shows the number of homes under contract fell 10.5% year over year, the greatest decline in nearly three years, as buyers pulled back.

“The market is cooling on both sides, but in different ways. Buyers are stepping back as higher mortgage rates cut into their buying power, while sellers are listing less often without a broad increase in delistings or price cuts,” said Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com. “We’re seeing a pause in new supply, but owners who already have homes on the market appear to be largely unphased.”

The national median list price was $415,000 in October, down 2.2% from a year earlier and marking the 12th consecutive month of annual declines. Active inventory grew for a fourth straight month, bringing the national supply gap to 6.7% below typical pre-pandemic levels—the narrowest gap since the pandemic, according to the report.

Realtor.com says the stock of homes under contract fell 10.5% year over year for a third consecutive monthly decline, the steepest annual drop since October 2023. Thirty-year mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, 110 basis points above a year earlier, putting added pressure on buyers’ purchasing power.

At the same time, 357,000 new listings came to market, down 7.5% from October 2025. Despite fewer new listings, active inventory reached 1,183,500 homes, up 7.4% year over year—the fastest annual growth in eight months. The year-over-year acceleration partly reflects a slower inventory comparison last fall; active listings have also risen each month since February. National inventory is now 6.6% below typical pre-pandemic levels, the narrowest gap since the pandemic.

Sellers did not respond to weaker demand with a broad wave of withdrawals, the report shows. The number of delisted homes rose 2.7% year over year, but the delisting rate— delistings as a share of active listings—held at 4.4%, compared with 4.6% a year earlier. The rate ticked up from about 4.0% in September, in line with the typical seasonal rise into fall.

Price cuts remained common, but their share eased from September. 20.5% of active listings saw their prices reduced in October, down 0.3 percentage points from the prior month and 0.2 points above a year earlier. The October share was the highest for the month since 2022 and the second-highest of 2026.

“Rates eased to 7.24% on Oct. 29, down from 7.40% in mid-October, but they remained 107 basis points above a year ago and 53 basis points above early September. That loss of purchasing power is showing up first in demand: The stock of homes under contract is down over 10% year over year, while the rate of contract signings fell 17% year over year,” said Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com.

As the market moves into the holiday months, the balance between inventory and prices will be an important test, writes Realtor.com. More homes for sale and slower sales can increase supply, but if sellers do not make deeper price cuts, buyers may not gain as much ground as inventory growth alone suggests.

“On the seller side, we see more of a pause than an exodus,” said Krimmel. “New listings are down at a time of year when activity is already seasonally low, but the share of listings with price cuts is only 0.2 percentage points above last year and slipped from September. We also haven’t seen a meaningful increase in delistings. As we approach the holidays, a seller pulling a listing around Halloween or Thanksgiving is not necessarily showing the same distress as one who exits in midsummer.”

“A well-timed offer with reasonable, season-specific requests has a much higher chance of acceptance when winter is around the corner,” says one real estate pro. Read more.

#5609. OpenAI to acquire developer tooling startup Pierre Computer

OpenAI Group PBC today announced plans to acquire Pierre Computer Company Inc., a low-profile developer tooling startup.

The terms of the deal were not disclosed. Observers pegged it as a shot at Microsoft Corp.’s open-source software repository GitHub for the age of artificial intelligence agents.

Pierre operates a cloud service that AI agents can use to store the code they generate. It can also store related files such as software licenses and interface design elements. According to Pierre, the service provides significantly better performance than competing technologies. It helped one customer, AI startup Lovable Inc., cut code retrieval latency by about 70%.

Pierre also develops a collection of popular open-source libraries. Two of those libraries, Trees and Diffs, underpin the interface of OpenAI’s Codex programming tool.

Large software projects contain upwards of hundreds of code files that are organized in dozens of folders. Many programming tools include a sidebar specifically designed to help developers navigate those folders. Trees, the first Pierre-developed library used by Codex, marks it easier to implement such sidebars.

Trees can equip a folder navigation sidebar with a search feature and drag-and-drop controls for moving subfolders. Additionally, it flags code files that have been recently added or updated. Developers review those files first when performing tasks such as troubleshooting an outage.

Diffs, the other Pierre library that OpenAI has integrated into Codex, is also designed to power programming tool interfaces. In particular, it can be used to implement the main interface that shows the code the user is currently editing.

When a code file is updated, Diffs points out the specific lines of code that changed to spare developers the hassle of manually finding them. It can show changes in a separate interface section or in-line.

OpenAI will continue to offer Trees and Diffs under an open-source license after the acquisition closes. Additionally, it plans to integrate the features of Pierre’s paid code hosting service into Codex. In the longer term, the Pierre team will help OpenAI “ship new products and platforms.”

The effort will place an emphasis on building software that can optimize coding agents. In particular, OpenAI hopes to streamline agent workflows that involve Git. That’s an open-source tool developers use to manage code files. Trees, Diffs and Pierre’s paid storage service all provide built-in support for Git.

OpenAI makes extensive use of the tool internally. On Monday, the company revealed that it has built a software engine called Pando to boost the performance of its internal Git environment. The engine reduces the amount of time it takes OpenAI engineers’ coding agents to create and read code files.

#5608. Americans cling to homeownership as affordability gap widens

New ACS data shows incomes up 3.9 percent, but buyers still need $110,700 to comfortably afford a median-priced home.

Americans are clinging to the dream of homeownership — even though their incomes are barely enough to sustain it.

The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year data on Thursday, which includes statistics on 40-plus topics, including housing. The national homeownership rate held steady at 65.3 percent, only 0.1 percentage points below the 5-year high of 65.4 percent. The majority of homeowners carry a mortgage (59 percent), with the real median mortgage payment increasing 2.4 percent year over year to $1,598.

Total housing costs, which may include expenses like homeowners association (HOA) fees, maintenance and repairs, increased 3.5 percent year over year from $2,090 to $2,163. Households now spend 21.9 percent of income on these costs, up 0.5 percentage points and just 8.1 points below the widely recognized 30 percent affordability threshold.

Median household incomes are edging up (+1.2 percent yoy after inflation), but Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones said it’s not enough to keep up with median home value growth.

“New 2025 American Community Survey data show median household income rose 3.9 percent to $84,780, with incomes up nominally in 49 of 50 states,” she said in an emailed statement. “But housing remained out of reach for many households. With a median listing price near $424,000 in 2025, mortgage rates averaging 6.6 percent, a 20 percent down payment, and taxes and insurance at roughly 1.7 percent of home value, a buyer needed about $110,700 to afford a median-priced home, roughly $26,000 more than the typical household earned.”

“Closing that gap would have required incomes to be 30.5 percent higher, prices about $99,000 lower or mortgage rates near 3.5 percent,” she added. “That affordability challenge has persisted, even as the year started with a promise.”

Jones said the market was primed in homebuyers’ favor at the beginning of the year, with sub-6 percent mortgage rates. However, macroeconomic and geopolitical conflicts have pushed mortgage rates up — now in the 7.30 percent range — leaving most homebuyers unable to take advantage of better inventory levels and falling list prices.

“Even assuming incomes have grown in line with recent wage gains of 3 percent to 4 percent since 2025, the typical household income would still be roughly $28,000 short,” she said. “Demand has cooled in response to higher rates, and pending sales fell 4.1 percent year over year in September, the steepest annual drop since March 2025, even as inventory approached pre-pandemic levels and prices softened.”

Realtor.com has released several reports on how homebuyers can attempt to make the math work, even as rates fluctuate. They can improve their credit scores, increase their down payments, shop lenders and build a budget buffer to help them absorb a 0.50 percent rate increase or decrease.

As for what lies ahead this year, homebuyers aren’t expected to receive mortgage rate relief.

The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady (at 3.75 to 4 percent) at its Oct. 28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. The federal funds rate affects how banks and financial institutions set rates, including mortgage rates, but a change doesn’t guarantee mortgage rates will move in tandem.

The 10-Year Treasury Yield has the greatest impact on mortgage rates as lenders add a spread — or percentage markup — on top of it. The spread reflects the effects of monetary and fiscal policies, economic growth, inflation, higher origination costs and the gap between mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and Treasury yields.

“Whether the Fed hikes or holds this month, homebuyers shouldn’t expect a big change in mortgage rates,” First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson told Inman on Wednesday after the Fed’s FOMC meeting. “With another hike widely expected in December and further increases possible next year, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated, keeping many buyers and sellers on the sidelines. But not everyone has the luxury of waiting. New jobs, growing families and other life events will keep some buyers moving forward, even as higher rates delay moves that can wait.”

Jones said mortgage rates will remain “the swing factor” and will shape next year’s American Community Survey results.

“For rates to trend lower, inflation has to cool, and the latest data shows it is moving the wrong way,” she said. “Annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September as energy prices surged amid the conflict in the Middle East, and core inflation edged up to 2.6 percent.”

“With the Fed focused on bringing inflation back under control while protecting the labor market, a significant drop in mortgage rates is unlikely in the near term,” she added. “For buyers on the fence, though, today’s mix of more inventory, more price cuts and more room to negotiate is the best they’ve had in years.”

#5607. Los Angeles Mayor-Elect Nithya Raman Vows To Triple Homebuilding To Improve Affordability

Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman has unseated the city's Democrat incumbent Mayor Karen Bass after running a campaign centered on affordability and housing.

The Associated Press called the election for Raman on Thursday afternoon as she widened her lead over Bass.

Bass, 73, called Raman to concede her loss and congratulate her successor on her victory.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken," the outgoing mayor said in a statement, in part. "I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us."

The win underscored a "blue wave" that swept Democrats into control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a decisive rebuke to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

When Raman, 45, takes office in January, L.A. will become the nation's second-largest city led by a democratic socialist, following in the footsteps of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Raman's swearing-in will expand a growing roster of democratic socialist mayors nationwide, including Janeese Lewis George in Washington, DC, Katie Wilson in Seattle, and David Morales, in Providence, RI.

Ahead of her victory, Raman appeared before a jubilant crowd of supporters at the Greek Theatre Plaza in Griffith Park Tuesday, arguing that L.A. voters were frustrated with Bass' record on cost of living and were demanding change, reported KTLA5.

"We watched friend after friend, family after family, leave because they couldn’t afford to stay here anymore. And we all talked about it as if these things were completely out of City Hall’s control," she told the audience. "That’s the cynicism that started to take over this city. That started to make us believe that L.A.’s problems weren't just bad, but they were permanent."

Raman ran a campaign focusing on housing, homelessness, and safety issues. The centerpiece of her platform was a plan to triple annual housing production by speeding up permitting through strict "shot clocks" for approvals.

Further proposals included overhauling inspections, updating codes, and eliminating additional fees to incentivize developers to build more starter homes.

""oday, less than 10% of the new homes built in L.A. are for-sale," Raman recently told Realtor.com®. "Under current city and state regulations, for-sale projects are charged higher fees, have a more-complicated approval process, are easier to appeal, and have increased liability risks for developers."

The 43-year-old councilmember was sharply critical of her mayoral predecessor, contending that Bass has not done enough to tackle L.A.’s yearslong housing crisis.

Bass’ record includes signing Executive Directive 1, which streamlined approval for roughly 50,000 units of fully affordable housing, overseeing a historic rezoning program to clear a path for building half a million new homes, adding more housing units to transit corridors and job hubs, simplifying the building application process, and updating rent stabilization rules for the first time in 40 years to shield tenants from steep hikes.

However, it was on Bass’ watch that Realtor.com Metro Report Cards released in September ranked L.A. the nation’s least affordable large city—a result that Raman did not find surprising.

"We’ve made it too difficult, time consuming, and costly to build homes in Los Angeles," concluded Raman.

Assuming a 10% down payment and a 6.5% 30-year fixed mortgage, a median earner in L.A. would have to spend nearly 85% of their income on monthly mortgage payments on a $1.12 million median-priced home, effectively putting ownership out of reach of all but the wealthiest buyers.

Beyond cost-of-living issues, Raman face pressure upon taking office to deliver on her lofty campaign pledge to reduce citywide homelessness by 50% in time for the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles.

Fulfilling that promise will be a major challenge, given that recent 2026 data showed roughly 45,000 people living in tents and encampments on the streets of L.A.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5606. Arista’s record quarter shows the network has become central to AI

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

The artificial intelligence buildout is well underway, with much of the focus on silicon and compute hardware. The network is treated as plumbing, something you connect after the important decisions have been made. Arista Networks Inc.’s strong third-quarter results signaled greater awareness of the network’s critical role, and Arista is well-positioned to benefit from this secular trend.

Arista reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, up 58.5% year over year and 20.5% sequentially. That is the fastest growth in the company’s history as a public company and well ahead of its $3.3 billion guide. Adjusted, non-GAAP earnings per share were $1.20, up from 77 cents a year ago. Gross margin was 64%, operating margin was 49.1%, and cash totaled $14.4 billion with no debt.

Management raised full-year 2026 guidance for the fourth time this year to about $13.3 billion, representing 48% growth. Fourth-quarter revenue is expected to come in between $3.9 billion and $4 billion. Arista also gave a first look at 2027, calling for 38% to 40% growth to about $18.5 billion. Within that, AI networking is expected to double from $3.5 billion to about $7 billion, and campus is expected to grow 60% to about $2 billion. The shares rose about 12% in after-hours trading, moderating to a 5% rise today.

Though investors will always gravitate toward the numbers as proof points, the commentary by Chief Executive Jayshree Ullal (pictured) was equally important. “We believe the industry is shifting from a compute-centric vertical stack to a holistic network-centric approach,” she said.

I agree, and the reason is economics. In large clusters, the network often determines how productive the AI factory is. When packets drop or a link fails, expensive accelerators sit idle, and inference makes the problem worse. Ullal described the move from “highly centralized training compute to disaggregated and distributed inference,” with prefill, decode, storage and KV cache spread across resources. “A well-designed network is becoming a foundational cornerstone for optimal token efficiency,” she said.

Buyers are getting it. Boards and chief financial officers now measure AI by cost per token and accelerator utilization, both of which depend on the network. A 5% gain in GPU utilization across a multigigawatt build is worth far more than the switches that delivered it. Once you understand that math, the network shifts from a commodity to a performance decision.

This awareness benefits every networking vendor, but it disproportionately benefits Arista for three reasons.

The first is accelerator diversity. Three years ago, Arista talked about four or five AI customers running 50,000 to 100,000 Nvidia Corp. graphics processing units, often on InfiniBand. Today, it has more than 100 Etherlink customers and expects more than 10 gigawatts of deployment across 10 or more types of accelerators by the end of 2027.

“In 2026, we are in a super cycle of AI,” Ullal said. “What a stark inflection in just three years.” Nvidia is a formidable networking competitor, and its Spectrum-X Ethernet has won over hyperscalers such as Meta Platforms Inc. and Oracle Corp. But Nvidia’s networking is optimized around its own full stack, and as customers bring Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Microsoft Corp.’s Maia, Meta MTIA, Qualcomm Corp., and Cerebras  Inc. silicon into production, many will prefer a network supplier that isn’t also selling a competing accelerator.

Every new accelerator expands the share of AI networking open to an independent Ethernet vendor, and Arista leads that category. Co-design work with Cerebras and Maia means Arista is now involved in system design rather than added afterward.

The second is scale-across. Power limits are forcing AI capacity to be spread across buildings and regions, and connecting those sites requires deep buffers, large routing tables and very high reliability. Ullal said scale-across accounted for about 30% of AI demand this year and should rise in 2027, with the 7800 platform as the anchor. “There’s just no room for error when you’re connecting millions of XPUs,” she said. This is where Arista’s routing and EOS software experience matter most.

The third is scale-up. Arista showcased rack-scale Ethernet designs at OCP, built on the Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking or ESUN specification, with trials in 2027 and production in 2028. Ullal compared it to the InfiniBand transition: Arista expects to move from “staring at proprietary UALink or NVLink” to “of course, it’s going to be ESUN.” If that happens, Arista’s market expands inside the rack, a segment it has never served.

Security strengthens the argument. Chief Technology Officer Ken Duda said Arista is working with Anthropic PBC, Google LLC and OpenAI Group PBC to integrate AI-driven vulnerability discovery into its software pipeline, including through Project Glasswing. As AI finds flaws faster, an operating system with process isolation and hitless patching becomes an advantage.

Ullal drew the contrast sharply: “Everybody else is dealing with a game of Whac-A-Mole where they’ve got thousands of vulnerabilities and no AVA can possibly keep track of it.” President and Chief Operating Officer Todd Nightingale said this “Glasswing and Mythos effect” is a major reason campus is growing so far ahead of the market.

The stock had fallen more than 20% in the month before the report, according to Chartmill, and analysts raised several concerns.

Deferred revenue. Total deferred revenue was flat at about $6.8 billion, which some interpret as a sign of slowing demand. CFO Chantelle Breithaupt said the balance had “the largest churn in and out” yet stayed flat while the company delivered 58.5% growth, and that the year-end balance will be higher than last year. Ullal said parsing it that way turns demand into “a physics problem,” adding, “We’re just in the best position we’ve been in a long, long time in my 18-year career at Arista.”

Spending and margins. Research and development jumped to $408.5 million from $278.1 million. Duda attributed the increase to hyperscaler prototypes and liquid cooling, and Breithaupt kept the long-term R&D range at 9% to 11% of revenue. Gross margin dipped from 65.2% a year ago, but Ullal held the long-term range at 62% to 64%, including for scale-up products.

Supply and visibility. Purchase commitments rose to $11.4 billion, and inventory to $3.2 billion. Multiyear agreements now cover silicon, circuit boards and memory. Regarding visibility, Ullal said that although Arista has two quarters of order visibility, “we have two years of work behind it.”

For several years, the debate over Arista has centered on whether Ethernet could displace InfiniBand. While InfiniBand will continue to play a key role in AI buildouts, Ethernet has much broader applicability, and its growth will outpace InfiniBand.

The new question is how much of the AI system the network will define, and this quarter suggests the answer is more than most expected. As accelerators multiply, inference spreads and AI-driven threats grow, value moves toward the layer that connects and protects everything. That is Arista’s layer.

Sebastien Naji of William Blair expressed a similar view in his earnings note. “As networking becomes a more important lever for improving performance and token output in AI data centers, Arista is well positioned to capture a growing share of spending across the most demanding AI workloads,” he wrote. “Combined with continued share gains at enterprises and neoclouds, we believe Arista’s expanding addressable market and competitive positioning support further upside in the coming quarters. We continue to view Arista as a core AI infrastructure holding and reiterate our Outperform rating.”

The biggest risk to Arista isn’t deferred revenue or market demand; it’s whether it can keep executing as crisply as it has as it gets bigger and demand accelerates But execution is something the company has excelled at under Jayshree Ullal.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5605. Amid ‘tough market,’ Rocket revenues are up

Rocket’s Q3 earnings, explained: Revenue, market share, Redfin metrics and the questions agents should be asking about the integrated model.

Detroit-based Rocket Companies on Thursday announced its third-quarter 2026 earnings, and despite being in what CEO Varun Krishna said “might be the toughest mortgage market in 30 years,” revenues increased.

The company generated net revenue of $3.28 billion and adjusted revenue of $2.57 billion; net income was $709 million and adjusted net income was $419 million. The company’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $748 million (a 29 percent margin, up from 28 percent from last quarter).

Rocket also reported $11.4 billion in liquidity (a record), including $2.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology.”

The company’s third-quarter net income compares with a $124 million loss in the same period of 2025.

“The market is literally testing every single lender,” Krishna said during the company’s earnings call Thursday. “If you have a strong business model, it’s gonna shine through, but if you have a flaw, it’s gonna get exposed.”

He pointed to Redfin as a source of new mortgage clients. “Redfin is the doorway to Rocket,” Krishna said. According to the company, the number of Redfin visitors who started a purchase mortgage from a listing rose 50 percent year over year. Cumulative unique listings displayed through Rocket’s partnership with Compass reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in the prior quarter.

Brian Brown, Rocket’s president, chief financial officer and treasurer, said the fourth quarter will come in well below the third, with refinance volume falling as much as 50 percent. Rocket expects adjusted revenue between $2.1 billion and $2.3 billion for the period. “The fourth quarter will be harder still,” Brown said. “We’re ready for it.”

In Q2 2026 earnings, Rocket Companies reported $2.78 billion in revenue for a $229 million profit, up from $34 million year over year. Company executives credited its broker partners with more than $2 billion in net rate lock volume through its Compass partnership, a three-year collaboration undertaken in February.

In March, Rocket and Redfin joined Compass International Holdings in writing an open letter to multiple listing service leaders, urging them to support phased listing distribution and stop fining agents for what they called “seller-directed marketing plans.”

Rocket Companies now encompasses Rocket Mortgage, the U.S.’s largest lender, which includes Mr. Cooper, the country’s largest mortgage servicer, acquired just over a year ago; Redfin’s brokerage and home search portal; Rocket Close, its title and closing company; and Rocket Money and Rocket Loans, its consumer finance brands.

Christy Murdock and Lucy Cohen Blatter contributed to this story.

#5604. Bobby Flay and Brooke Williamson Reveal What It’s Like To Have 2 Celebrity Chefs in a Home Kitchen—and How They’re Prepping for Thanksgiving

Food Network chefs Bobby Flay and Brooke Williamson are getting ready for another Thanksgiving celebration at their beautiful Hamptons home, and they've shared their best tips and tricks ahead of the holiday.

In an interview with People magazine, the power couple said that their best advice is to start dinner prep early.

“Prep as much as you can ahead of time,” said Williamson, 48. “I think stuffing tastes better the next day, once it’s had a chance to meld together.”

Flay, 61, dropped another helpful piece of advice: “Have chicken stock on your stove. It reheats the sliced turkey, which ultimately gets dried out no matter what you do. It can also thin out gravy that gets too thick.”

While one might assume that having two celebrity chefs in a household can feel like a case of too many cooks in the kitchen, the duo said it’s never a problem for them.

“We definitely split up the work,” said Williamson. “It never feels like we’re in each other’s way. It feels like it makes sense.”

Flay and Williamson invited the publication into the kitchen of their New York City home, showing off the gorgeous cabinets and generously sized island.

After a recent trip to Italy, the couple told the magazine that they’re planning a Tuscan-inspired feast this year, joking that it’ll be a “mini ‘Brady Bunch’” scenario with their blended families. Flay is dad to 30-year-old Sophie, while Williamson has a son, Hudson, 18.

In September, Flay spoke about the home kitchens he has in his two residences—his Tribeca pad and an estate in the Hamptons.

“The kitchen is spacious, and I make three meals a day in there,” he told The Wall Street Journal. ”The space relaxes me and allows me to cook for family and friends.”

In his home out East, the kitchen is not just a place to whip up delicious meals. The room functions more like a full-fledged restaurant.

“On the other side of my sizable island are three French cafe tables for guests,” he explained. The setup is even equipped with a professional fryer, which he described as a “recent kitchen splurge.”

Among his latest kitchen tools is a utensil he’s relied on for years: “I still have the chef’s knife I used at [the French Culinary Institute],” he shared. “When [I] prepare food with it, the feel reminds me that I’m still learning every day."

The kitchen of the Amagansett home is his favorite place to cook and where he has typically hosted Thanksgiving.

Flay built the dwelling from the ground up during his marriage to “Law and Order: SVU” actress Stephanie March. The former couple, who divorced in 2015, hosted a turkey dinner for a staggering 50 guests at their first Thanksgiving in the home.

“I prepared two 30-pound turkeys and cooked sides for days,” he recalled in a 2013 interview with Elle Decor. “I stand at my kitchen island from the minute I get out here to the minute I leave.”

Although Flay has publicly discussed his desire to steer clear of matrimony after three divorces, he and Williamson have agreed on an alternative way to show their commitment to each other.

“She’s like, ‘I just want a big ring and a big party,’ and I was like, ‘I love that idea because my marriages have not lasted, unfortunately,’” he told People.

Explaining that the “most important thing” is to “make sure that Brooke feels like she’s committed to,” he recalled of the moment he gifted her a “giant diamond ring” during a trip to London.

Williamson describes the flashy piece of jewelry as “the perfect ring,” adding that “it’s very sparkly.”

Although she was initially thrown off by the gesture, she now sports the rock on her right hand.

“I thought it was incredibly thoughtful,” said Williamson. “He said just because I don’t feel the need to get married or want to get married again doesn’t mean that you don’t deserve the big, beautiful ring that comes along with it.”

While Flay has been private about his past relationships, he admits he’s been more open this time around, and cites all they have in common for his “confidence” about their partnership.

“I feel very confident about this,” he said of the pair’s connection. “There’s so many wonderful things about it.”

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5603. AI agents meet billable hours as Certinia rethinks services delivery

Certinia Inc. is bringing AI into the software firms use to sell projects, assign staff, deliver work and bill clients.

AI’s ability to instantaneously draw from a deep well of information and provide guidance in practically any field of expertise has changed the paradigm for professional services. For Certinia Inc., whose business facilitates 7.1 billion professional services operations per month, AI represents a significant opportunity for its clients.

“I think the only industry that’s probably been more disrupted by AI than the technology industry has probably been the services industry,” Robert Cesafsky, chief operating officer of Certinia, told theCUBE. “Whether you are a software company, a hardware company, a tax and accounting firm [or] management consulting … all of these industries are being directly targeted or impacted by AI. Whatever your strategy is, you need to be able to have the right tools. You need to be able to have control of that services business, and that’s what Certinia provides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s coverage of the Certinia at Dreamforce event. (* Disclosure below.)

Certinia launched in 2009 as FinancialForce.com Inc., a cloud-based accounting and enterprise resource planning provider built natively on the Salesforce Inc. platform. It rebranded in 2023 as it broadened from accounting and ERP to managing services businesses.

Certinia’s Salesforce-native platform connects a wide range of processes spanning sales, project delivery, financial management and customer success. The company’s approach helps clients transform cost centers into profit centers by improving visibility into customer activities, optimizing resource deployment and maintaining connectivity throughout the customer lifecycle.

“We can take away all the administrative tasks and outsource that to AI in order to help them deliver faster time outcomes, but it also helps them deliver a lower cost to serve that project,” said Mimi Spier, chief marketing officer of Certinia, in an interview with theCUBE. “We can identify expansion opportunities, [and] at-risk customers where we need to optimize renewals. Everything we’re doing is ultimately affecting the bottom line.”

Certinia’s long-time relationship with Salesforce is a key element in the company’s overall strategy. Certinia is featured under the AI agents and tools category for Salesforce’s AgentExchange and has provided AI-powered sales and delivery for Salesforce’s consulting partner network.

“We have a deep partnership with Salesforce,” said Raju Malhotra, chief product and technology officer of Certinia. “I spend personally a lot of time with the Salesforce executives on business and engineering, and we collaborate. We bring our customer use cases, they tell us about what’s coming up from a capability perspective and we work very well together. They’re led by a founder [chief executive officer] who’s very much in tune with the market, and they want to stay ahead.”

Certinia has sought to stay ahead in its own right by introducing Veda, an enterprise-grade intelligent operations engine that functions as the company’s suite of AI specialist agents and intelligent actions. The solution delivers rules-bound, trusted and ROI-focused autonomous workflows, combining Certinia’s years of institutional memory with advanced AI reasoning. Certinia’s goal with Veda is to provide customers with enough flexibility so that agents integrated into existing business workflows can drive immediate and measurable value.

“We’ve infused Veda throughout the experience for users to be more productive,” Malhotra said. “We have packaged agents, which are Veda agents. We launched Veda with 10 packages. Now we have 24, and we will finish the year with more than 40 packaged agents. Those agents are very much persona based, and they help our customers.”

Veda is not simply a layer of generic automation; it represents a key shift in how AI is being used in the enterprise. Certinia’s focus on serving the professional services market motivated the company to ground its AI offering in operational reality, where context, coordination and control matter as much as speed, according to Scott Hebner, principal AI analyst at theCUBE Research.

“Certinia’s recent announcement of Veda is more profound than it may appear on the surface,” he said. “Veda is notable not simply because it introduces a new suite of AI agents and intelligent workflow-based actions, but because it offers a glimpse into what the future of enterprise AI is likely to look like: AI that works alongside humans in consequential workflows, helps people make better decisions and earns trust by being grounded in business context, governance and real operational outcomes.”

Since the launch of Veda in April, Certinia has taken several actions to enhance its AI capabilities. In July, the firm acquired Moonnox, an AI-native services delivery platform purpose-built for the professional services sector.

This acquisition added a contextual layer to Veda through knowledge graphs, persistent project memory and services-specific agents. The combined platform can now connect a new client request with approved scope, staffing requirements and financial impact, then recommend governed actions for professional review, according to Hebner.

“Certinia provides the deep, structured foundation of professional services, customer success and financial management; Moonnox brings the missing half: capturing the unstructured reality — the emails, chats, and calls — where delivery actually happens,” he explained. “Together, they fuse everything a services business knows with everything their teams do, moving Veda beyond orchestration toward context-aware, AI-native services delivery.”

The context graph can also draw on structured records such as timecard entries and utilization figures. Moonnox helps bring that information into the graph for client-facing teams managing projects, according to Cesafsky.

“That’s been where Moonnox has really showed up for us over the last couple of months,” he said. “It’s those capabilities to help the client-facing services [and] delivery teams run and operate their projects. [Moonnox] is effectively an intake machine for a lot of that structured data to bring that into the context graph as well.”

In September, Certinia unveiled its System of Action for services businesses. The offering significantly expanded the Veda AI suite with new agents and more than doubled the Veda Intelligent Actions library from 64 to 135.

Certinia’s System of Action uses a three-tier architecture to bring AI agents into services workflows. The first tier brings together structured records and unstructured project data. The second draws on more than 17 years of Certinia’s experience in services to inform decisions. The third lets agents act within existing workflows.

“We want to accelerate the delivery for our customers,” Malhotra said. “Our customers are solving some specific problems in the professional services world. We don’t want to just give you a project plan. If you choose to execute that project plan with some agents, we’ll give you that. If you want to really think about agentic capabilities to help you in making money, in expanding your time [and] in terms of delivery, we will help you with that.”

For professional services firms, adopting AI agents means deciding which parts of project delivery to delegate to them.

“We view professional services as a leading indicator of where enterprise AI is heading because it combines knowledge-intensive work, dynamic context, collaborative decisions, measurable economics and human accountability,” Hebner said. “If Certinia executes well, Veda could become an important blueprint for translating digital labor into economic outcomes.”
