#5572. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5571. Aina’s smart AI ring promises a new way to interact with AI agents that anticipate user’s needs

Artificial intelligence has come a long way in a very short space of time, writing emails, answering questions, generating code, images, video and more besides. But as breathtaking as these advances are, using AI is still a hassle. People have to dig out their smartphone and find the right app, then enter a prompt before anything gets done.

Seeking to eliminate this friction is a startup called Aina Computers Inc., which has just emerged from 15 months in “stealth mode” to launch its flagship product: an AI-native smart ring equipped with an OLED display that’s purpose-built to control autonomous AI agents.

Aina founder Apoorv Shankar told SiliconANGLE that the development of hardware interfaces has not kept pace with the advances in AI. For people to access intelligence, they need to go fumbling through smartphone applications or switch on a laptop.

Even the most basic tasks, like ordering an Uber, require someone to open an app, enter their destination and click to confirm. To join a virtual meeting, the user still has to dig through their emails to find the right link. In Shankar’s view, AI is trapped behind a software layer and that means it cannot proactively serve people when they need it.

Aina’s Ring is meant to free AI from these binds and make it as simple to access as uttering a command. The Ring is made from titanium and comes equipped with a colorful OLED display, a microphone and a speaker, and an 18-hour battery. There’s also a mechanical “shifter” that can track thumb gestures in four directions.. “We started building Aina with a thesis that AI would evolve from following instructions to anticipating what we need,” Shankar explained.

The device is powered by Aina’s Context Aware Operating System software, which is designed to learn the Ring wearer’s behavior over time in order to anticipate their needs. It can connect to the user’s devices, such as their smartphone and computer, and also any AI agents they use. Once it’s up and running, it tries to anticipate what users will need at any given moment and surface the information they need on the Ring’s display before they even ask for it.

“With proactive agents, this shift has already begun,” Shankar said. “Agents like Muse, Instinct and Dots will soon run hundreds of our daily tasks, yet we still have to instruct them by text or voice. But soon, they’ll learn our patterns, build on our context and turn proactive for almost every interaction, waiting only for our approval.”

Shankar founded Aina last year. The startup was originally a human-computer interaction research lab. Its 40-person team experimented with dozens of different hardware concepts, including an adaptive three-key Mac keypad called Dune, before ultimately settling on the Ring as the ultimate interface for AI agents.

Aina’s $399 Ring is available for pre-order now and will ship to customers in January. That’s the date at which people’s relationship with AI is set to fundamentally change, Shankar believes. When someone wears Aina’s Ring, the way they interact with their AI agents will generally become a matter of simply saying yes or no, for they will quickly learn to anticipate what their users need, at the moment they need it, he said.

Users can interact with the Ring in three ways. The microphone is there to support voice interactions. The user simply presses and holds the button in the center to call up an agent and instruct it to do something, or else they can just use it to record some quick notes. It will also be able to relay phone calls, enabling people to converse by just holding their hand close to their ear.

The Ring also supports cues that are powered by the context-aware operating system. As it learns to anticipate user’s needs, it will be able to proactively order an Uber ride based on the time of day, their location and their schedule. All the user has to do is click or say “yes” to confirm and the Ring will book the ride. Alternatively, if someone is late for an appointment, the Ring will proactively draft a message to let the person they’re meeting know when they’ll arrive.

Shankar said the Ring can also be used as a remote control, so if someone is watching TV they’ll be able to tell it to pause or rewind the show they’re watching. It can adjust microphones and cameras during video calls, skip to the next track when someone’s listening to music on their iPod and so on.

“Every major shift in computing has come from software and hardware built together,” Shankar said. “The mouse and GUI brought us personal computing. The touchscreen and the app gave us mobile computing. Now with Aina we enter a new era, with personalized computing right at your fingertips.”

#5569. NEAR Protocol Tokenomics Overhaul Catapults The Crypto Coin 10% Higher

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

NEAR Protocol is climbing as the market weighs a major tokenomics overhaul designed to reduce token inflation and ease long-term selling pressure. The NEAR rally follows crypto governance approval of a proposal to lower the network’s annual issuance ceiling from 2.5% to 1.6% over two years.

The proposal, known as HSP-029, passed with overwhelming support from NEAR’s House of Stake. It would gradually reduce the number of new tokens entering circulation, potentially strengthening the supply outlook as the network expands.

NEAR Plans to Take Millions of Tokens Out of Future IssuanceNEAR Protocol's (@NEARProtocol) $NEAR House of Stake has approved a proposal to reduce maximum annual token issuance from 2.5% to 1.6%.The change will roll out gradually over 24 months, reducing the issuance ceiling… pic.twitter.com/pmPOUrWhoI

The move comes as NEAR Protocol seeks to turn its growing ecosystem activity into stronger value for token holders. With issuance cuts, cross-chain infrastructure, and renewed trading interest converging, we are watching if NEAR can sustain its latest breakout.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The approved proposal would reduce NEAR’s maximum annual issuance rate from 2.5% to 1.6%, with the change phased in over 24 months. According to the proposal, the reduction could prevent 11.8 million NEAR from entering circulation during the first two years. Over six years, the avoided issuance could reach 66.1 million tokens.

At full implementation, daily issuance would fall from roughly 89,500 NEAR to 57,300 NEAR. The network would retain its existing distribution of newly issued tokens, with 90% going to staking participants and 10% allocated to the protocol treasury.

The overhaul also introduces a trade-off for stakers. Gross staking yields could decline from approximately 5.27% to 3.37%, assuming staking participation remains unchanged.

However, the proposal still requires Security Council review, a 90-day grace period, and validator adoption before the changes become binding.

Beyond tokenomics, NEAR Protocol continues developing its chain-signature technology, which allows accounts to interact with external blockchains. NEAR Intents also supports cross-chain swaps, giving the ecosystem another potential source of activity and fee revenue.

The combination of lower issuance and expanding utility is giving NEAR crypto bulls a fresh narrative. However, the market will need to see sustained demand before the supply reduction translates into a lasting price trend.

NEAR Protocol’s cross-chain ambitions arrive as Bitcoin infrastructure projects compete to bring more functionality to the world’s largest cryptocurrency.

Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is positioning itself as a Bitcoin Layer-2 network designed to support faster transactions, lower fees, and smart-contract functionality. Its architecture aims to connect Bitcoin’s security and liquidity with applications typically associated with more flexible blockchain ecosystems.

Bitcoin Hyper has begun rolling out testnet infrastructure, including a wallet and explorer, as it prepares for broader network testing.

Did somebody order a little extra Bitcoin utility? 👀⚡️https://t.co/VNG0P4FWNQ pic.twitter.com/bQAMiOcdUD

While NEAR Protocol is building cross-chain functionality across multiple networks, Bitcoin Hyper is focusing directly on expanding Bitcoin’s role in decentralized finance. This could become important if Bitcoin holders increasingly seek access to applications, trading, and other on-chain opportunities without moving away from BTC-focused infrastructure.

The project is approaching its planned November 26, 2026, launch, with its presale entering the final stretch. Bitcoin Hyper has raised more than $33.2 million, while HYPER is priced at just $0.0136.

The project also offers staking rewards of 35% APY, adding another incentive for early participants ahead of its anticipated token launch.

With the presale scheduled to end on November 26, the approaching launch is becoming a key milestone for HYPER holders watching for exchange listings and ecosystem growth.

NEAR crypto is trading around the $3.80 area, leaving the $4 level as an important near-term hurdle. A sustained move above $4 could strengthen the recovery narrative and open the door toward the $4.30 region. A stronger breakout could bring the $4.50 area into focus, particularly if broader altcoin sentiment improves.

The tokenomics overhaul gives bulls a fundamental catalyst, but traders will also need to see stronger spot demand and improving market momentum.

On the downside, a failure to hold the $3.70–$3.80 area could expose NEAR to another test of support near $3.50. Continued weakness across the broader crypto market would make a sustained recovery more difficult.

For now, NEAR Protocol has a clear catalyst in its issuance reduction proposal, alongside continued development of its cross-chain ecosystem. The next stage of the crypto rally depends on whether buyers can turn the tokenomics story into sustained demand and push NEAR beyond its immediate resistance levels.

#5568. Absolute Home Mortgage, First Option leaders on strengthening their partnership

Absolute Home Mortgage and First Option Mortgage described a strategic equity partnership positioned as neither a merger nor an acquisition. Executives said the combined platform targets about $4 billion in annual originations and includes about 420 producing loan officers.  AI Summary

On Wednesday, Absolute Home Mortgage Corp. and First Option Mortgage announced a strategic transaction that combines the companies’ resources and aims for originations growth amid a consolidating market.

Matthew VanFossen, the CEO of New Jersey-based Absolute, and Alvin Shah, managing partner at Georgia-based First Option, sat down with HousingWire shortly after the announcement to offer further details.

The deal, which combines the two companies with Mortgage Equity Partners — a wholly owned subsidiary of Absolute — is positioned to originate about $4 billion annually across roughly 420 producing loan officers. The leadership team will also expand as Shah and Kurt Nikolai, president and managing partner at First Option, join Absolute’s ownership group and board of directors.

Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Neil Pierson: This transaction is not considered to be a merger or acquisition. How would you describe it?

Matthew VanFossen: It’s lane three. Alvin and I, when we do business together, we never go down the two traditional paths. You could do mergers, you could do you asset sales, or we could have a buy-in situation. Usually it’s one company taking over another, but this is First Option, the business partner, buying a piece of Absolute Home Mortgage in an equity deal.

Maybe the headline should have been First Option acquires part of Absolute Home Mortgage, because that’s what’s going on. Absolute is the surviving entity in the transaction, but First Option’s brand will be alive. Their entire team will be onboarded. Alvin and Kurt are joining the board of directors and have an ownership share in the entity — of course, pending regulatory approval.

Alvin Shah: Obviously there’s a much bigger picture in mind. For me personally, we were looking for an exit strategy for my partner Kurt over the next several years anyways, so that was top and center in terms of what was going through my head. But the opportunity to work with the Absolute team, it’s not something new. I mean, we’re already partners in a technology company, Mortgage Automation Technologies.

Pierson: What is some of the history behind your partnership?

Shah: Matt started the BIG Point of Sale several years ago, and because of the Lenders One network, I was exposed to it. And when we saw what he was building, it was great. It’s a point-of-sale system built by lenders for lenders, so we jumped on board right away. We made an investment into the company.

It kind of forced Matt’s hand, allowing me to be on the board of directors over there as well. So we’ve all been working together for three, four years now. When everything transpired with First Option and what we were looking for long term, and also knowing what Matt was building long term in terms of the previous acquisitions he was involved in, the fit made sense right right away. I wanted growth, he wanted growth, and we knew what kind of damage we can do when we work together.

The question was, will the cultures within the organizations match? Unbelievably, it was such a great fit where the leadership at First Option and the leadership at Absolute, we almost immediately became just like family. Now, it doesn’t hurt that we’ve been friends and partners for so long, so a lot of the things that we did from a process standpoint, and from a vendor and technology standpoint, were already in line for both companies. So change from that standpoint was minimal.

Pierson: Can you provide more perspective on what appears to be the start of more deals to come? What do you look at when thinking about growing through M&A or equity partnerships?

VanFossen: Typically, for the the past four transactions we’ve done, I led up the M&A efforts. I would do the due diligence on the relationship management, the financials, but it’s not my strongest suit. I might have been a little lucky.

My strong suit is looking at technology and vision for the future — what we should be bringing in-house, what we should be developing. We have strategic partnerships on the board of directors that we have to be looking at. We’re doing business with multiple mortgage companies. I quickly learned that Alvin was better a better deal-maker than I am. He was better at sorting out the strategic numbers, the fits, the technology alignment.

Part of these past three or four years, we got our companies 90% in line with the same vendors, just from saying, “Hey, these vendors work.” We wanted to get our workflows very similar through our relationships in the industry. When we look at that, Alvin is better suited than I am to be our chief strategy officer, to go out and be working through the vendor networks, figuring out where the alignment is. Because how do you change everything with not changing much for the end user? That’s how you have retention, in our eyes.

When we look at these strategies, yeah, we’re probably not going to buy a company that’s not on the same LOS as us, because that’s too much disruption, right? But when we go to companies and we say, “OK, these are our vendors that are in line together,” this means that your staff would have minimal disruption.

When you look at our new board of directors at Absolute, we’re all staying in our lanes. My job is everything that comes tomorrow — five to seven years from now — and steering the ship in the right direction. Alvin’s job is growth and making sure that the machine is continuing to add.

Shah: I’ve been an owner of a brokerage before leveling up to become part of First Option and then eventually owning First Option. I’ve seen different tiers, and I’ve seen the industry change because I’ve been in the business for 24 years. I know what kind of a situation people are in today because I was in it before.

Looking at what the next several years of our business is going to do — and knowing what shoes other people are in — it’s easy for me to be able to dissect and show somebody, “Look, here’s what’s happening because of your scale, because of the size of your company, and here’s how I was able to solve for that problem.”

The bottom line of the company needs to be healthy and everybody within the organization needs to have opportunity. On the flip side of it, at some point, I would think to myself, “How do I get to the next level in my career?” And that’s another value proposition that now we’re able to present, because we’ve created what I call the Absolute group of companies.

If somebody has $30 million, $40 million, $50 million worth of production under them, and they want to do their own thing but they’re pigeonholed wherever they are — now we’re we’re giving them the platform to say, “Run your own company, build your own brand, be the president of your company.” But use the resources we’ve already established for you and the scale power.

When you’re a smaller company and you’re negotiating, you’re not negotiating. The vendors are in the driver’s seat. But when you’re a bigger company and part of a bigger platform, you essentially get the benefit of the bigger company. And now you’re able to feed into that, really build something and focus your attention on the things you really like doing.

#5567. Oracle’s multicloud approach: Put the database wherever AI pipelines already run

Enterprises racing to put AI agents into production are learning that real-time data pipelines matter as much as the models. An agent working from a stale subset of corporate records delivers far less than one wired into live, mission-critical data.

That shift is changing how companies decide where their databases run. Oracle Corp. has pushed its database modernization strategy into other clouds, and customers are moving databases next to the applications and AI pipelines they are building, according to Nathan Thomas (pictured), senior vice president of product management for Oracle Cloud Infrastructure at Oracle.

“Customers are defining their AI pipelines, I think from an enterprise business perspective, with an eye towards trust, with an eye towards security,” Thomas said. “They are really looking at, ‘How do I get the mission-critical data into those pipelines?'”

Thomas spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how real-time data pipelines help improve agentic AI performance. (* Disclosure below.)

Oracle offers its database on its own cloud, on-premises through Cloud@Customer and inside Amazon Web Services Inc., Microsoft Corp.’s Azure and Google LLC’s Google Cloud. Customers rarely ask which cloud to pick, since existing relationships and the location of their applications usually settle the question, Thomas explained.

“They’re usually saying, ‘Hey, I’ve already got a relationship. Let’s put the database where my apps are and where my AI pipelines are,'” Thomas said.

Running the same Exadata hardware everywhere also takes the sting out of migration. AI projects are adding value to database migrations, and a like-for-like hardware move avoids most of the refactoring that once made them so painful, he noted.

“I’m coming from on-prem on an Exadata. I can move into the cloud on an Exadata,” Thomas said. “It’s the same hardware, same environment, same tools, same management, same performance.”

#5566. Nelnet Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results

LINCOLN, Neb., Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nelnet (NYSE: NNI) today reported GAAP net income of $76.2 million, or $2.13 per share, for the third quarter of 2026, compared with GAAP net income of $106.7 million, or $2.94 per share, for the same period a year ago.

Net income, excluding derivative market value adjustments1, was $67.9 million, or $1.89 per share, for the third quarter of 2026, compared with $107.3 million, or $2.95 per share, for the same period in 2025.

"We delivered strong operating performance this quarter, with continued progress diversifying our products and customer base," said Jeff Noordhoek, chief executive officer of Nelnet. "We increased our dividend and continued to repurchase shares, while remaining focused on investing in our businesses and creating long-term value. In October, we announced FACTS Compass, which will help scholarship granting organizations support students in public and private schools through the new Federal Scholarship Tax Credit. BenefitEd offers employers a payroll deduction option for the program. We also announced the acquisition of Entab, a school management technology provider in India, expanding our education technology business internationally."

Nelnet operates through three divisions: Nelnet Financial Services (NFS), Loan Servicing and Systems [referred to as Nelnet Diversified Services (NDS)], and Education Technology Services and Payments [referred to as Nelnet Business Services (NBS)]. NFS includes the company's Asset Generation and Management (AGM) and Nelnet Bank reportable operating segments, which earn interest income on loans and investments. NDS and NBS generate primarily fee-based revenue through loan servicing, education technology, and payment services. Business activities not included in these divisions are combined and reported within Corporate Activities.

As of September 30, 2026, AGM's loan portfolio totaled $7.63 billion, consisting primarily of federally insured loans originated under the Federal Family Education Loan Program ("FFEL Program" or FFELP). During the three months ended September 30, 2026, AGM acquired $3.23 billion of consumer loans, including $3.06 billion of short-duration Pay Later receivables that the company began to purchase in August 2025, compared with $1.52 billion of consumer loans acquired during the same period in 2025. The company's consumer loan portfolio increased to $1.30 billion as of September 30, 2026, from $840.7 million as of September 30, 2025.

The AGM operating segment reported loan and investment net interest income of $65.2 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026, compared with $44.7 million for the same period in 2025. The increase was primarily driven by higher loan spreads2 and growth in the company's consumer loan portfolio, partially offset by continued runoff of the legacy FFELP portfolio. The average balance of AGM's FFELP loan portfolio declined to $6.46 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026, from $8.25 billion for the same period in 2025. During the first nine months of 2026, AGM contributed certain student loan trusts to Nelnet Bank that included $780.7 million of FFEL Program loans.

AGM recorded a provision for loan losses of $34.5 million ($26.2 million after tax) for the three months ended September 30, 2026, compared with a negative provision of $7.4 million ($5.6 million after tax) for the same period in 2025. The provision in each period was significantly impacted by the initial allowance established on loans acquired during the period to reflect lifetime expected credit losses under the current expected credit loss (CECL) methodology. During the third quarter of 2025, the company also reduced its allowance (and recognized negative provision expense) of $28.9 million ($22.0 million after tax) related to consumer loan sales.

AGM holds interests in joint ventures engaged in the acquisition, ownership, and management of loan portfolios. During the three months ended September 30, 2026, AGM recognized income from these joint ventures of $12.4 million ($9.4 million after tax).

AGM recognized income of $4.8 million ($3.6 million after tax) during the third quarter of 2026 related to changes in the fair value of derivative instruments that do not qualify for hedge accounting.

AGM reported net income after tax of $33.9 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026, compared with $27.8 million for the same period in 2025.

Net income, excluding derivative market value adjustments, is a non-GAAP measure. See "Non-GAAP Performance Measures" at the end of this press release and the "Non-GAAP Disclosures" section below for explanatory information and reconciliations of GAAP to non-GAAP financial information.

Loan spread represents the spread between the yield earned on loan assets and the costs of the liabilities used to fund the assets.

As of September 30, 2026, Nelnet Bank had a loan portfolio of $1.70 billion and an investment portfolio of $1.64 billion, and total deposits, including intercompany deposits, of $2.81 billion. Loan and investment net interest income increased to $20.4 million during the third quarter of 2026, compared with $15.4 million for the same period a year ago, due to growth in the loan and investment portfolios, partially offset by a decrease in net interest margin.

Nelnet Bank recorded a provision for loan losses of $4.8 million ($3.6 million after tax) in the third quarter of 2026, compared with $3.8 million ($2.9 million after tax) for the same period in 2025.

Nelnet Bank recognized income of $6.2 million ($4.7 million after tax) during the third quarter of 2026 related to changes in the fair value of derivative instruments that do not qualify for hedge accounting.

Nelnet Bank recognized net income after tax of $12.0 million for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, compared with $4.6 million for the same period in 2025.

Revenue from the Loan Servicing and Systems segment was $139.8 million for the third quarter of 2026, compared with $151.1 million for the same period in 2025. The company recognized $5.3 million and $32.9 million of revenue in the third quarters of 2026 and 2025, respectively, related to Department of Education (Department) contract modifications for services previously performed. Excluding this revenue, segment revenue increased year over year, primarily due to the acquisition of NDS Canada in the first quarter of 2026, which contributed $16.5 million of revenue during the third quarter. As of September 30, 2026, the company was servicing $523.6 billion in Department, Canadian, FFELP, private education, and consumer loans for 15.4 million borrowers.

The Loan Servicing and Systems segment reported net income after tax of $12.5 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026, compared with $35.2 million for the same period in 2025.

Education Technology Services and Payments

For the third quarter of 2026, revenue from the Education Technology Services and Payments operating segment was $132.9 million, compared with $129.3 million for the same period in 2025. Revenue less direct costs to provide services during the third quarter of 2026 was $83.4 million, compared with $79.0 million for the same period in 2025.

Net income after tax for the Education Technology Services and Payments segment was $19.4 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026, compared with $19.0 million for the same period in 2025.

During the three months ended September 30, 2026, the company recognized an unrealized loss of $9.3 million ($7.1 million after tax) from changes in the fair value of certain marketable equity securities.

The 2025 results included a gain of $30.2 million ($23.0 million after tax) related to a venture capital investment that completed an equity raise during the third quarter.

During the first nine months of 2026, the company has repurchased 731,932 Class A common shares for $93.7 million (average price of $128.04 per share), including a total of 415,332 Class A common shares for $53.1 million (average price of $127.81 per share) during the third quarter of 2026. Subsequent to September 30, 2026 (through November 5, 2026), the company repurchased an additional 295,990 Class A common shares for $37.0 million (average price of $125.04 per share).

Board of Directors Declares Fourth Quarter Dividend

The Nelnet Board of Directors declared a fourth-quarter cash dividend on the company's outstanding shares of Class A common stock and Class B common stock of $0.36 per share. The dividend will be paid on December 15, 2026, to shareholders of record at the close of business on December 1, 2026.

"Derivative market value adjustments" includes both the realized portion of gains and losses (corresponding to variation margin received or paid on derivative instruments that are settled daily at a central clearinghouse) and the unrealized portion of gains and losses that are caused by changes in fair values of derivatives which do not qualify for "hedge treatment" under GAAP. "Derivative market value adjustments" does not include "derivative settlements" that represent the cash paid or received during the respective period to settle with derivative instrument counterparties the economic effect of the company's derivative instruments based on their contractual terms.

The accounting for derivatives requires that changes in the fair value of derivative instruments be recognized currently in earnings, with no fair value adjustment of the hedged item, unless specific hedge accounting criteria are met. Management has structured all of the company's derivative transactions with the intent that each is economically effective; however, the majority of the company's derivative instruments do not qualify for hedge accounting in the consolidated financial statements. As a result, the change in fair value for the derivative instruments that do not qualify for hedge accounting is reported in current period earnings with no consideration for the corresponding change in fair value of the hedged item. Under GAAP, the cumulative net realized and unrealized gain or loss caused by changes in fair values of derivatives in which the company plans to hold to maturity will generally equal zero over the life of the contract. However, the net realized and unrealized gain or loss during any given reporting period fluctuates significantly from period to period.

The company believes these point-in-time estimates of asset and liability values related to its derivative instruments that are subject to interest rate fluctuations are subject to volatility mostly due to timing and market factors beyond the control of management, and affect the period-to-period comparability of the results of operations. Accordingly, the company's management utilizes operating results excluding these items for comparability purposes when making decisions regarding the company's performance and in presentations with credit rating agencies, lenders, and investors. Consequently, the company reports this non-GAAP information because the company believes that it provides additional information regarding operational and performance indicators that are closely assessed by management and represents what earnings would have been had these derivatives qualified for hedge accounting. There is no comprehensive, authoritative guidance for the presentation of such non-GAAP information, which is only meant to supplement GAAP results by providing additional information that management utilizes to assess performance.

The tax effects are calculated by multiplying the realized and unrealized derivative market value adjustments by the applicable statutory income tax rate.

#5565. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

#5564. CCM’s non-solicitation push tests limits of lender control

CrossCountry Mortgage has sent cease-and-desist letters to at least 25 former loan officers, invoking two-year non-solicitation clauses and seeking payments for allegedly diverted loans. Attorneys say non-solicits have long existed but were often used as a deterrent because litigation is costly and proof is hard.   AI Summary

CrossCountry Mortgage’s enforcement of non-solicitation agreements is emerging as a test case for how far lenders will go to protect production in a higher-for-longer rate environment — a topic that has divided the industry.

The top-five mortgage lender has sent cease-and-desist letters to at least 25 former loan officers, invoking a two-year non-solicitation window and demanding thousands of dollars in payments under their employment agreements, HousingWire reported Friday. CCM declined to comment on this story.

Non-solicitation provisions, which restrict departing employees from taking the former employer’s clients, referral partners or staff, have long been part of mortgage recruiting playbooks. But attorneys and executives say many lenders – mainly smaller ones – do not enforce them because litigation is costly and proof can be difficult.

That calculation may be shifting as origination volume remains compressed, margins stay thin and experienced producers become more valuable in a smaller market.

“With this high-rate environment continuing, top LOs will still be highly sought after, so they have to be careful on what type of agreements they enter into with a new company, what they own or not when they enter into those agreements” said Colgate Selden, a founding member of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and a shareholder at Baker Donelson. “The companies hiring them have to be careful what they accept from the old company, if anything.”

Alan Pezeshkian, president of House America Financial, said every company has a version of a non-solicitation, but in practical terms, it’s more of a deterrent to the extent that companies enforce it.

“You’ll probably see that happening more now as volume has gone down, so companies have the time, resources and perhaps the need to make sure that they protect their organization and their assets. We have that clause but have I enforced it? No,” he said. “On one hand, you want to convey a message in the industry of where you stand. On the other hand, if you enforce it, you become a villain.”

“I still think that CCM was singled out for a practice that is common and widespread,” said Paul Hindman, an industry consultant whose clients include CCM, adding that the distinction between sending notices and pursuing a legal case is important.

To reduce the risk of these disputes, top or more sophisticated loan officers and ‘plug-and-play’ branches are increasingly negotiating exceptions that let them own the leads they personally generate, which are then carved out from the definition of company property. Other agreements spell out differences between in-house leads provided and funded by the lender and those generated by an LO’s own marketing, open houses or personal sphere, so those contacts can be solicited after a move.

Refinance opportunities often fall into the in-house category, because they typically come from the lender’s past customer database and corporate marketing campaigns. Several CCM letters reviewed by HousingWire specifically reference refi business.

That dividing line — who truly owns the customer relationship — is now at the heart of the recruiting and enforcement battle.

Brendan McKay, owner of McKay Mortgage, argues that originators hold the relationship, but concedes the picture changes when the company bought and supplied the lead.

“Threatening loan officers with lawsuits for continuing to serve clients whose trust they personally earned is not only anti-loan officer, but it’s also anti-consumer. It’s time for our industry to start writing employment agreements that recognize the difference,” McKay said.

One caveat: Hindman said employment agreements have expanded from simple two-page documents to “30 pages of legalese,” which makes it harder for loan officers to fully understand what they are signing. Still, he said, LOs cannot ignore contractual terms once they have accepted large financial packages to join.

“You can’t take a million-dollar sign-on bonus and say that you’re not going to do certain things, and then do those things and object to being called out for it,” Hindman said, adding that originators should be clear with borrowers up front when contractual restrictions could limit their ability to keep working together after a move.

Whether a non-solicitation clause can be enforced can come down to who is initiating contact and how the provision is drafted, with outcomes varying by state. Cases in which a loan officer actively reaches out to former customers are generally viewed more favorably for enforcement, attorneys said.

“But when the borrower is approaching the loan officer, that’s looked at a lot differently because you don’t want to restrict consumers – consumers have the right to choose who is going to do their loans, and you can’t go ahead and have an agreement that binds them,” said James Brody, managing partner at Brody Gapp. “When the borrowers reach out, I would have a hard time thinking that a court would go ahead and enforce that.”

Ron Gapp, founding partner at Brody Gapp, added: “When you start saying borrowers can’t approach somebody, it now is becoming a non-compete, and those are two different regimes. Definitely, a non-compete is going to have a lot more scrutiny than a non-solicit would.”

In the brokerage channel, some firms are rewriting agreements in response to LO pushback. Todd Bitter, national director of sales for NEXA Lending, said the company changed its contracts after new hires flagged language claiming ownership of their databases for 12 months after they left: “It’s not NEXA’s to own; it is yours because the loan officer should own their database,” Bitter said.

He described non-solicitation agreements as especially common among retail mortgage lenders, though some brokerages use them as well. Bitter also questioned whether lenders should rely on aggressive restrictions simply because they can.

“Is it legal? Yes. Is it right? No,” he said, adding that many cease-and-desist letters appear designed as scare tactics, even if they never lead to court. “But who wants to find out?”

The same tensions are emerging around referral partners. Some non-solicitation agreements extend to real estate agents and other referral sources, attempting to bar them from directing business to a departed loan officer. But, according to Brody, those provisions are on shaky ground.

“You can’t abridge the rights of third parties with regards to your contracts, and attempt to go ahead and stop those third parties from being able to have the freedom to use the loan officer or company of their choice,” Brody said. “This is something that would be looked at very sternly.”

A top mortgage broker who requested anonymity said the imbalance of resources between large lenders and individual loan officers turns cease-and-desist campaigns into “corporate bullying.” Major shops can afford to send repeated letters and pursue litigation if they choose, while former employees must weigh the cost, time and stress of hiring counsel or risking default, this source added.

CCM’s letter seeks repayment calculated at 75 basis points per loan for loans LOs originated that allegedly violated their agreements. Attorneys say that figure likely represents a rough estimate of the company’s lost economics — essentially the split CCM would have retained if the production had remained in-house, or a “haircut” on profitability. But they caution that originators need to understand exactly what any such formula is tied to.

“When you have a provision in a contract that acts as liquidated damages, you have to look at whether or not it’s a reasonable anticipation of those losses, with some facts behind it, or whether it starts to look like a penalty,” Brody said. “If it looks like a penalty that’s divorced from those specifics, then courts will routinely strike those down because you’re not allowed to have a liquidated damages provision that acts as a penalty.”

Brody also mentioned that switching the burden of proof “in and of itself would need to be analyzed and shouldn’t really be opined off the cuff.”

#5563. Automated Logic Signs Agreement to Acquire Logical Solutions, Inc.

Advances Carrier's ability to deliver solutions for intelligent, autonomous and efficient buildings in key verticals and expands its national presence in strategic markets

KENNESAW, Ga., Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Automated Logic Contracting Services, Inc. (Automated Logic), a leading provider of innovative, intelligent building-management solutions and a part of Carrier Global Corporation (NYSE: CARR), global leader in intelligent climate and energy solutions, today announced that it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Logical Solutions, Inc. (LSI), an Automated Logic dealer headquartered in Richardson, Texas. The strategic move adds significant additional scale, technical expertise and capabilities, including field engineers, project managers, application engineers and service professionals, to Automated Logic's growing national footprint alongside the recent acquisition of Control Consultants & Services, Inc., an Automated Logic dealer with offices in Lubbock and Abilene, Texas.

LSI's proven expertise in mission-critical environments enhances Automated Logic's ability to deliver solutions for intelligent, autonomous and efficient buildings by accelerating digitally connected solutions and increasing customer proximity across the lifecycle. This acquisition adds to Automated Logic's extensive field network across the Americas, building on its successful integration of six acquisitions in response to customer demand.

Delivering end-to-end intelligent building solutions, LSI's deep expertise combines seamlessly with Automated Logic's enterprise automation platform, accelerating the creation of unified, AI-ready building-management systems that drive efficiency and performance.

"LSI has built a strong business through technical expertise, customer focus and flawless execution excellence," said Gaurang Pandya, President, Climate Solutions Americas, Carrier. "We are excited to have LSI join the Automated Logic team, building on a relationship that dates back to 1995. Together, we will support the growing needs of scale customers in mission-critical environments across North America through our Carrier QuantumLeapâ¢ suite of solutions."

"Joining Automated Logic represents an important next chapter for LSI," said LSI owners Jim Barber, Ben Blackerby and Daniel Tarver. "Our organizations share a long history, and this combination creates new opportunities while preserving our focus on employees, customers and quality execution."

The transaction is expected to close in the coming months.

About Automated Logic Automated Logic provides innovative building-management solutions that maximize energy efficiency and sustainable building operation while ensuring comfort. Its intuitive products control and monitor building functions such as heating, air conditioning and lighting for commercial office, education, health care, government and data center markets through a global network of independent dealers and field offices. Automated Logic is a part of Carrier Global Corporation, global leader in intelligent climate and energy solutions, committed to creating innovations that bring comfort, safety and sustainability to life. For more information, visit www.automatedlogic.com or follow Automated Logic on LinkedIn.

#5562. What to expect during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA: Join theCUBE Nov. 10-12

Kubernetes has emerged as the default container orchestration standard, a foundational platform layer across the enterprise. Will Kubernetes also play a central role in positioning the next generation of AI workloads for production?

This is the question on the minds of the cloud-native community as it gathers this month for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA in Salt Lake City. With the rise of AI agents that have progressed from answering user questions to executing code and running business systems, customers are increasingly interested in controlling what autonomous agents are allowed to do.

“That brings us to OpenShell, an open-source secure agent runtime that Red Hat is helping develop alongside Nvidia and, of, course, the broader community,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante, during a pre-event interview. “The approach puts enforcement into the environment where the agent operates, setting boundaries around what it can access and execute rather than relying on a model alone to follow the rules. We think this is a central question for the next chapter of cloud native: how do enterprises give agents enough freedom to be useful without giving up control?”

During KubeCon + CloudNativeCon, Nov. 10-12, theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio, will feature on-site reporting and exclusive interviews with executives from Red Hat Inc. and Nvidia Corp., among others. TheCUBE will examine the latest innovations in GPU orchestration, agentic workloads and platform engineering as inference and autonomous agents move into production. (* Disclosure below.)

OpenShell, while still an early-stage project, is actively being developed for Kubernetes environments. The activity reflects growing customer interest in using containerized environments for applications, according to theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty.

“Fifty-one percent of organizations report that 51–75% of their applications now run in containers, representing a sharp rise from just a few years ago,” Nashawaty said. “Organizations now run the majority of their applications in containers which is a sharp rise that reflects the accelerating cloud-native transformation central to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon.”

OpenShell was accepted into the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a sandbox project in September. One component of OpenShell allows agents to run in isolated sandboxes with limits on the files they can reach, an approach actively supported by the cloud-native community within the Kubernetes ecosystem.

“It builds on top of some core Kubernetes special interest groups,” said Pete Cheslock, principal AI community architect at Red Hat, during an interview with theCUBE. “The Agent Sandbox is one of them so that you can deploy these agents in a secure way using Kubernetes APIs.”

Cheslock’s point about security highlights the growing concerns and recent publicity surrounding AI agents and their ability to break out of isolated environments and compromise systems. Rapid enterprise adoption and integration of AI are increasing the risk profiles for organizations, a topic that will be on the agenda for KubeCon + CloudNativeCon.

“Our research data reveals that 41.3% of organizations cite increased vulnerability risk as the top security challenge, introduced by faster CI/CD cycles and a tension that cloud-native teams are increasingly turning to Kubernetes-native tooling to resolve,” Nashawaty said.

Enterprise reliance on cloud-native tools and open-source software requires confidence that these technologies are safe to use inside enterprise infrastructure. In May, Red Hat and IBM Corp. unveiled Project Lightwell, a $5 billion commitment to help enterprises secure open-source software.

“For the last year, especially since the Mythos moment, [security] has been the first thing that we’ve talked about in every customer conversation I’ve had,” said Stu Miniman, senior director of market insights for hybrid platforms at Red Hat, in conversation with theCUBE. “We’re trying to make sure that customers can feel secure and understand and use these tools. There’s even more effort being put on security than ever, which has always been a focus of Red Hat. If we don’t make sure that layer is as locked down and reliable and trusted as possible, everything else becomes secondary.”

At this month’s KubeCon gathering, theCUBE will explore how various practitioners are using Kubernetes to ensure workload portability across multicloud environments. Companies such as Vultr and ScaleOps are building Kubernetes-based tools that can support a range of platforms, reflecting enterprise computing trends.

“With our AppDev research finding that 94% of organizations now operate across two or more cloud providers, the demand for consistent, developer-friendly Kubernetes-based platforms has never been more pressing,” Nashawaty explained.

KubeCon also offers an opportunity to assess the progress of key technology projects under the CNCF umbrella. One of the major contributors in this arena has been Google LLC, which contributed the open-source service mesh Istio, serverless building blocks via Knative and Kubernetes itself. KubeCon is an annual reminder of how large the CNCF ecosystems has become, according to Red Hat’s Miniman.

“They’ve got a big ecosystem. I can give example after example of who created these technologies,” Miniman told theCUBE. “Oh yeah, the GitOps stuff came out of Intuit, and the platform engineering stuff came out of Spotify. Just find your focus and go in there, because there is no way you can cover all of it.”

Don’t miss theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA from Nov. 10-12. Plus, you can access theCUBE’s exclusive content on demand after the event.

We offer various ways for you to watch theCUBE’s coverage of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, including theCUBE’s dedicated website and YouTube channel. You can also get all the coverage from this year’s events on SiliconANGLE.

SiliconANGLE’s “theCUBE Pod” is available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube, which you can enjoy while on the go. During each podcast, SiliconANGLE’s John Furrier and Dave Vellante discuss the biggest trends in enterprise tech, including AI, cloud, cybersecurity and infrastructure, with context and analysis.

SiliconANGLE also produces our weekly “Breaking Analysis” program, where Vellante examines major developments in enterprise tech, combining insights from theCUBE with spending data from Enterprise Technology Research, available on Apple Podcasts, Spotify and YouTube.

At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, theCUBE will speak with Red Hat leaders and other industry executives about the latest innovations in GPU orchestration, agentic workloads and platform engineering as inference and autonomous agents move into production.

#5560. CFPB narrows enforcement practices, closes 86% of supervisory actions

The CFPB said it is narrowing supervisory and enforcement activity, closing 86% of open supervisory actions and cutting scheduled exams by about 50%. It is also reviewing ability-to-repay and mortgage servicing rules, along with revised fair lending and Section 1071 requirements.  AI Summary

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) said that it is narrowing its supervisory and enforcement activities and closing most of its outstanding supervisory actions, as well as pursuing changes to mortgage lending and servicing rules, according to its latest semi-annual report, released Oct. 27.

The report, which covers the first half of 2026, outlines the bureau’s efforts to align its work with the Trump administration’s priorities.

During the broader reporting period of July 2025 through June 2026, the CFPB closed 1,327 of the 1,552 supervisory actions that were open as of July 1, 2025, or approximately 86%. The bureau said the closures reflected either institutions sufficiently addressing the issues or findings that no longer aligned with its priorities.

The CFPB also reassessed all 80 open examinations and closed 66 that did not align with its revised priorities. The remaining 14 continued with a focus on correcting violations, addressing compliance weaknesses and providing relief to affected consumers.

The bureau also reduced the number of scheduled examinations by approximately 50%, shifting its attention toward depository institutions, activities it deemed actual consumer fraud and areas within its statutory authority. Mortgage origination and servicing remain among its supervisory priorities.

Under its new approach, the CFPB said examinations will focus on clearly identified products and potential violations tied to specific laws and regulations. The bureau also plans to avoid duplicating oversight already conducted by state or other federal regulators.

The CFPB is pursuing several mortgage-related regulatory changes under President Donald Trump’s executive order on promoting access to mortgage credit. Among its priorities is a review of the ability-to-repay requirements and qualified mortgage definitions under Regulation Z. The bureau is evaluating whether to modify the requirements, which apply to most residential mortgages.

The CFPB is also considering a final rule to streamline mortgage servicing requirements under Regulation X. The proposal, initially issued in July 2024, is intended to simplify the loss-mitigation review process and make it easier for servicers to assist borrowers who experience payment difficulties.

In July 2026, after the report’s primary reporting period, the bureau also issued a request for information seeking feedback on ways to promote access to mortgage credit.

The CFPB additionally finalized changes to its fair lending and small-business lending rules. In April, the bureau amended Regulation B, which implements the Equal Credit Opportunity Act. The rule removed longstanding language supporting disparate-impact liability and revised restrictions on discouraging prospective credit applicants.

It also prohibited for-profit creditors from using race, color, national origin or sex as eligibility criteria for Special Purpose Credit Programs.

A separate May rule revised requirements for small-business lending data collection under Section 1071 of the Dodd-Frank Act. Among other changes, it lowered the annual revenue threshold for businesses covered by the rule from $5 million to $1 million, removed certain data collection requirements and extended the compliance date to Jan. 1, 2028.

The bureau said it did not cite any fair lending violations during the reporting period, and that while it continued investigations, it instead focused its efforts on cases involving intentional discrimination with identifiable victims. It also made no referrals to the Department of Justice for potential patterns or practices of lending discrimination.

Overall, the CFPB said it closed approximately 40% of its pending investigations as part of its effort to align enforcement with its revised priorities.

The bureau reported receiving approximately 8.27 million consumer complaints between July 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026. It sent approximately 7.5 million complaints to companies for review, and companies responded to 99.6% of those complaints.

The report’s complaint figures come as the CFPB has moved to limit the public availability of consumer complaints. In August, the bureau said it would stop publishing unverified complaint narratives and related data visualizations in its public database, arguing that the accounts present only one side of a dispute and may not reflect violations of law.

The bureau also said it would continue collecting complaints, reviewing company responses and sharing information with regulators. Previously published narratives will remain available through its Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) reading room.

#5559. Same model, better answer: Enterprise data is what turns generic AI into a business tool

Generic AI models can write SQL, but they don’t know a company’s orders, customers or revenue definitions. Now, Oracle Database aims to give AI agents the context to move a stalled order forward.

But that shift raises questions about complexity, lock-in and security as AI agents start acting on live transactions. Oracle Corp.’s answer is a converged platform that keeps vectors, graphs, documents and transactions in one engine, according to Hasan Rizvi (pictured), executive vice president of product and research, database engineering, at Oracle.

“If you ask a generic AI assistant, you get a generic answer,” Rizvi said. “If you ask an AI assistant that knows your business, you get a much better answer. Where is the stock? How can I fix the transaction? How can I expedite the delivery?”

Rizvi spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed database convergence and the safeguards needed for AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)

AI lets teams spin up applications and data stores very quickly, making data sprawl everybody’s problem. Skeptics favor specialized databases for each workload, but new data types built inside Oracle’s engine inherit proven availability, security and scale, according to Rizvi.

“We’ve been working on this engine for 40 years, which is highly available, highly secure, highly scalable, highly performant,” Rizvi said. “If you build a new data type or a new workload in the same engine, you get all that benefit, multiple decades’ worth of investment.”

Choice is the other half of the pitch. The database runs on-premises, through Oracle Cloud@Customer and across multiple public clouds, and Oracle used the event to expand Iceberg support in its Autonomous AI Lakehouse, Rizvi noted. But security is where AI raises the stakes most, with Oracle’s Deep Data Security defining access policies in the database itself, so a user’s identity travels with every request from an agent or AI-generated app.

“Before, it took a lot of time and effort to find vulnerabilities to exploit them,” he said. “Now, with AI, it’s made it very easy to reverse engineer fixes for attackers to attack.”
