#5558. Florida’s Amendment 3 could give housing market a ‘sugar high’ through year-end

Florida voters approved Amendment 3 with 62%, raising the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Agents expect accelerated buying and residency decisions ahead of the 12/31/2026 cutoff, with uneven effects by market and inventory type.  AI Summary

Jason Haber, a Compass broker licensed in both Florida and New York, believes the Sunshine State’s approval of Amendment 3 will lead to the state’s housing market experiencing a “sugar high” to close out the year.

Amendment 3, which was approved by 62% of the electorate on Tuesday, easily surpassing the 60% threshold, increases the homestead exemption, reducing the taxable value of a person’s primary residence in the state. Prior to this, homeowners could receive an exemption of up to $50,000, but the amendment increases the exemption on non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Beyond that, the amendment says the exemption will be adjusted for inflation.

This means that if someone’s primary residence has an assessed value of $350,000, in 2028, the new $250,000 exemption would leave $100,000 subject to non-school property taxes, assuming the homeowner qualifies for the full exemption, generating potentially thousands of dollars in savings for homeowners.

Haber agrees that the amendment could create “serious property tax savings for those who homestead in Florida.”

“That was clearly very attractive to the majority of people. Affordability is the top domestic issue of our time right now and people see this as direct relief on their cost of living,” Haber said.

But the amendment comes with a caveat. Homeowners must establish primary residency in Florida before Dec. 31, 2026, in order to be eligible for the 2027 and 2028 exemptions. If you establish primary residency after the deadline, you will have to wait five years until you’re eligible for the expanded exemptions, which is why Haber believes the market may experience a “sugar high.”

“If you were on the fence this would certainly move you to act quickly,” Haber said, noting that Florida uses a variety of “carrots” to entice people to move to the state.

Chris Wands, the founder of The Wands Team, a RealTrends Verified ranked team, at Douglas Elliman, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, shares a similar view.

“It may make people move faster especially if they are already planning to move in the first half of next year,” Wands said. “I think it makes Florida an even more attractive state. A lot of people are moving here for the tax benefits, so adding another benefit helps with that.”

If a “sugar high” market does happen, local real estate professionals said it could have greater impacts on some markets than others.

“In Boca Raton right now, if a house is priced properly, you will have six people fighting over it, but that isn’t the case in every market. Further north in the state, the market is weaker because those markets are more impacted by high interest rates, so it would be a different story there,” Haber said.

Danielle Blake, the chief of residential and advocacy at Miami Realtors + RWorld, shares a similar view.

“Availability of inventory is going to vary by the asset class that you are looking for, whether it is single family or condominiums, and also the geographic location. In Miami, we have more condo inventory than single-family inventory at affordable price points, but that also varies by cities. Some cities have a larger supply, so it really varies,” Blake said.

In addition to a potential uptick in new residents, Wands also believes this could impact current primary residents’ decisions on purchasing larger properties, especially if they were previously concerned about how property taxes could impact their long-term affordability. This could then open up more mid-level or entry-level properties, helping more people get into the housing market.

Blake however, is skeptical, noting that despite this impacting the property tax portion of the affordability equation, many current homeowners may be reluctant to give up the 3% mortgage rate they have on their current property, especially in today’s mortgage rate environment.

In addition to this, property taxes in Florida are reset when a property is sold, meaning that if the purchase price goes up, so do the property taxes.

“Even if you’re not paying as much as you otherwise would have, anything that pushes up purchase price and, by extension, property taxes can have that adverse impact on affordability,” Haber said.

Additionally, legislators could increase the millage rate, which would hamper the affordability benefits homeowners are hoping to gain out of this amendment.

Beyond impacting homeowners, Wands also noted the amendment’s provisions relating to investment properties could also help renters.

Under Amendment 3, the annual cap on increases in the assessed value of non-homestead properties drops from 10% to 5%. This means that if a rental property’s assessed value is $300,000, the existing 10% cap would generally allow its assessed value to increase by as much as $30,000 in a year. Under the new 5% cap, that increase would be limited to $15,000.

“I think it puts guard rails up for renters and investment property owners by giving them more stability in what they can expect their taxes to be,” Wands said.

If Florida sees an influx of homebuyers set on establishing their primary residency prior to the Dec. 31, 2026 cut off, it would naturally have an impact on other housing markets as the buyers have to come from somewhere. Unsurprisingly, many are pointing to New York City as a market that could be impacted by the amendment’s approval.

“The year-end residency cut off is going to bring a lot of decisions,” Frances Katzen, the founder of The Katzen Team, a RealTrends Verified team, at Douglas Elliman, said. I’m going to be watching for people who are going to downsize their primary home here, keeping a small apartment as a base, but moving their primary residence to Florida. But that move doesn’t necessarily mean giving up a connection to New York.”

Katzen said she wouldn’t predict a mass exodus from the Big Apple based on this amendment alone.

“Buyers are not stupid,” she said. “They are going to weigh the full cost of ownership, including insurance, which is very expensive in Florida, along with maintenance and condo assessment fees, alongside family and business ties. This could influence the timing of a move but a property tax break alone won’t determine where people build their lives.”

On Wednesday, Florida’s Governor Ron DeSantis called a special session that will focus on some of the implementation language surrounding the amendment, so until then it remains to be seen exactly how this will impact the state’s housing market in the future. In the meantime, agents are prepping for a flurry of activity to close out the year.

“I’m getting a lot of emails and phone calls today from people asking about how they can qualify by the December 31 cut off,” Blake said.

What Blake is most excited about is how the amendment could impact future generations of homebuyers who have grown up in the state or lived there most of their lives, as it would immediately decrease the property tax portion of their housing affordability concerns.

While Amendment 3 could provide a short-term boost to Florida’s housing market, its longer-term impact will depend on how the tax changes are implemented and whether the savings are enough to offset rising home prices, insurance costs and mortgage rates.

#5556. Can the new Congress help lower mortgage rates?

After a Democratic midterm win, lawmakers may try to ease drivers of inflation tied to oil, AI investment, tariffs, and jobs. The Fed is likely to respond mainly through how these factors move the 10-year yield and inflation expectations.  AI Summary

After the Democrats’ historic midterm win, the question now is: can the new Congress help get mortgage rates lower? Obviously, the Iran conflict and trade war have taken their toll on President Trump’s approval ratings, but can Congress — both Democrats and Republicans — now work together on getting something done that the President will not veto?

Let’s look at the economic factors influencing rates in this environment, what Congress can do about each, and how the Fed might consider these as they set monetary policy.

When WTI oil was at $112 on April 7 this year, the 10-year yield was at 4.31% — but back then the Fed was still talking about cutting rates two to three times. A lot has changed since then.The Federal Reserve has made the Iran conflict a big talking point, so some type of resolution to this conflict could impact rates. Obviously, the conflict has hurt President Trump and the Republicans; it’s very unpopular, especially with farmers and truckers who have to deal with high diesel prices. Trump himself acknowledged the war played a major part in the midterm results.

Congress made some attempts to try to end this conflict in the past, but may have renewed incentives now to find a solution. We shall see what comes next, as President Trump has said he could make a deal after the midterms.

Now, the AI boom is a little bit more complicated because there are a lot of projects still in the pipeline that can’t be shut down by the Democrats right now, but future projects could definitely be affected. And with some type of regulation and moratorium, some of the growth prospects might be slowed down.

This is a critical factor because the Federal Reserve has really made the AI boom and inflation a hot topic. It’s part of the reason why, when you see AI softness — whether it’s the credit markets or their stock prices getting hit — bond traders tend to want to buy bonds, not sell them, in that environment. For now, the Fed needs to see a material slowdown to lose its hawkish stance on AI, but it would be another positive for rates.

On another note, the labor productivity data was awesome today. This data really affects how the Fed sees AI and will be the best news for mortgage rates if this trend continues. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh himself has made a dovish case around AI as long as it creates more productivity and lowers labor unit costs.

Here is the chart of the 10-year yield for the last six months as of this second, the 10-year yield is down once again to 4.83% as AI stocks are selling off.

This will be very interesting because I am sure President Trump will try every legal angle to continue his tariff policy — he still wants to have tariffs because it’s his favorite tool to cut deals. However, what the midterms have done is limit the power he can have to escalate the trade war into something worse. That can be a very big positive: we might have seen the high of the 10-year yield at 5.35% if the trade war doesn’t get worse amid the conflict with Iran.

For now, we need to wait and see how much farther the President wants to push the trade war. He might just cut a deal with Canada, leave other countries alone and just focus on China — which would be a positive for rates.

Usually, in an economic cycle, when manufacturing jobs and construction jobs are being lost, it’s not a good sign for the labor market: we saw that in 2025. But the labor market has improved this year and that has kept the Fed’s focus fully on inflation.

One thing to think about going forward is that, if we do have some data center moratoriums and rates stay elevated, construction labor might get hit a little bit harder than before the midterms. If the unemployment rate rises as growth slows down, that will be a positive for mortgage rates.

For rates to really make a meaningful move lower and stick, three of the four things above need to get better. You need to get oil prices trading between $67 and $82. You need to get diesel prices down so the Fed won’t talk about energy prices being passed onto the consumer. You’ve got to de-escalate the trade war 2.0 and get some deals in and not make it inflationary.

The AI moratorium and regulations will be a welcome signal to the Federal Reserve; whether that impacts the construction data enough to matter to them is still an open question, but the three things above need to occur to have rates go under 7% and stay there.

#5555. Rice breaks ground on the Arc in the Ion District, expanding Houston's innovation ecosystem

Nearly 200,000-square-foot research hub will connect Rice, industry and entrepreneurs to accelerate discovery, collaboration and commercialization

HOUSTON, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Rice University broke ground on the Arc in the Ion District, a nearly 200,000-square-foot research, corporate innovation and office building designed to bring researchers, industry leaders, entrepreneurs, investors and top talent together to accelerate innovation and move ideas from discovery to real-world application.

Located in Houston's Ion District powered by Rice, the Arc will feature seven floors of flexible, future-ready lab and office space for Rice and other organizations seeking proximity to leading research, highly skilled workers and Houston's dynamic innovation ecosystem. Rice will be a lead tenant, occupying nearly 80,000 square feet, or about 40% of the building.

"The Arc is a significant investment in Rice's future and in Houston's continued growth as a center for innovation," said Robert T. Ladd, chairman of the Rice Board of Trustees. "It will create new opportunities for industry leaders, researchers and students to work together on ideas with the potential for lasting impact."

The Arc will share a plaza with the Ion building, extending the 12-block Ion District and placing researchers in close proximity to companies, startups, investors and entrepreneurs.

"The Arc will bring Rice's extraordinary research and talent and Houston's impactful innovation ecosystem into even closer connection with the industries and innovators working to solve some of the world's most consequential challenges," said Rice President Reginald DesRoches. "That constant exchange of ideas and expertise will help move discoveries more rapidly from the laboratory to real-world impact."

Built for advanced research and collaboration

The facility will offer flexible lab and office environments that can adapt to evolving research and business needs. Floor plates will range from 28,000 to 31,000 square feet, with 15-foot floor-to-floor heights and infrastructure capable of supporting advanced HVAC, high-capacity electrical and emergency power systems and core laboratory requirements.

The building will also include conference and meeting spaces, an amenity lounge, fitness center, outdoor plazas, underground parking, secure bike storage and on-site retail and dining â creating opportunities to build solutions in the lab, develop partnerships across the district and connect informally throughout the day. The project is designed to meet LEED Gold criteria and will incorporate smart-building and energy-saving features.

"We are creating more than a high-performance business and research building," said Kelly Fox, Rice executive vice president for operations, finance and support. "The Arc is being designed as a destination where companies can access sophisticated infrastructure, connect with one another and build the relationships that lead to new ideas and opportunities."

Work within the building will span areas including artificial intelligence and machine learning, data science, robotics, quantum science and engineering, energy and more.

The groundbreaking event comes on the heels of the university's recent announcement of a transformational universitywide AI initiative to recruit 75 faculty members working across disciplines and expand AI-related courses and degrees. The initiative is accelerating Rice's emergence as a global leader in advanced computing and responsible AI.

"The closer researchers are to the people confronting real-world problems, the more opportunities there are to identify important questions, test ideas and improve solutions," said David Sholl, Rice executive vice president for research. "The Arc gives us an environment built specifically for that kind of sustained collaboration."

Rice's new AI Foundry will be located inside the Arc, where faculty AI experts will have offices and work with industry partners to tackle complex challenges, rapidly develop practical solutions and help organizations build long-term AI capabilities.

The effort will address a growing challenge: AI is advancing faster than many traditional industry innovation models can adapt. Instead of relying on lengthy, linear development cycles, the Foundry will bring Rice experts and industry partners together to identify high-value opportunities, design and test solutions, deploy them in real-world settings and continually refine them based on results.

The Foundry is envisioned to support organizations through AI readiness assessments, feasibility studies, proofs of concept, deployment-ready solutions, executive education and customized workforce training.

"The AI Foundry is exactly the kind of collaboration the Arc is designed to enable," said Amy Dittmar, the Howard R. Hughes Provost and executive vice president for academic affairs. "By bringing Rice researchers together with industry partners in a shared environment, we can accelerate the movement of ideas from research into practical applications while helping organizations build the capabilities they need to succeed as AI continues to evolve."

Responsible AI is a key catalyst in Momentous: Personalized Scale for Global Impact, Rice's strategic plan, which also calls for strategic faculty growth and specifically identifies cross-disciplinary cluster hiring as a way to build depth and breadth in areas vital to the university's future. The institution's four AI cluster areas are foundational AI; two applied areas including AI for health and AI for energy, the environment and resiliency; and responsible AI: society and ethics.

The Arc will complement the Ion building, the namesake centerpiece of Houston's innovation corridor and home to corporate and industry partners including Chevron, Microsoft, Aramco, ExxonMobil, Oxy, Shell, United, Transocean and Woodside Energy.

Co-working space in the Ion managed by Industrious is fully occupied, with more than 250 member companies. Activate, an organization that scientists and engineers become founders and move research toward commercialization, recently launched its third cohort of fellows. Twenty-five startups have participated in the program to date.

Companies based in the Ion, including Persona AI, CES Renewable, Greenflash Infrastructure and Cognite, also have experienced significant growth, reinforcing the building's role as a home for emerging companies and technology-driven organizations. The Ion's development also extends beyond offices and laboratories. MADabolic, a strength-training gym, recently opened in the building. Greentown Labs, Community Artists' Collective and Pickle Lab are also among the organizations that call the district home.

Together, the Ion and the Arc are intended to create a more connected environment where researchers, entrepreneurs, established companies and the broader Houston community can work, meet and exchange ideas.

"Houston has an extraordinary concentration of industry expertise, capital, talent and entrepreneurial energy," said Bobby Tudor, Rice alumnus and chairman of the Houston Energy Transition Initiative. "The Arc will help turn that concentration into action by creating more opportunities for breakthrough research to become technologies and companies."

The project is being developed by Rice Real Estate Co. Construction is expected to be completed in the second quarter of 2028. Preleasing opportunities are now open for companies and organizations interested in locating alongside Rice researchers and joining the broader Ion District ecosystem.

For more information, visit https://www.thearciondistrict.com/.

Rice has highly respected schools of architecture, business, continuing studies, engineering and computing, humanities and arts, music, natural sciences and social sciences and is home to the Baker Institute for Public Policy and Kinder Institute for Urban Research. Internationally, the university maintains the Rice Global Paris Center, a hub for innovative collaboration, research and inspired teaching located in the heart of Paris, and Rice Global India in Bengaluru, India. With 4,793 undergraduates and 4,185 graduate students, Rice's undergraduate student-to-faculty ratio is just under 6-to-1. Its residential college system builds close-knit communities and lifelong friendships, just one reason why Rice is ranked in the top 10 for best quality of life by the Princeton Review.

#5554. Oracle wants to pull stalled AI agents out of demo mode and into production

Companies want AI agents faster than they can build the AI architecture to run them. Most can put together a convincing demo. Far fewer can move agents into production without exposing data, hurting uptime or blowing their budgets.

That gap is pushing database providers to rethink what a data platform for agents has to deliver. Nearly 70% of organizations plan to deploy AI agents, yet very few get them into production, according to Çetin Özbütün (pictured), executive vice president of product and research, data warehouse and autonomous database, at Oracle Corp.

“AI is very easy to demonstrate, but when you try to bring it into production, enterprises usually encounter four different deployment difficulties,” Özbütün said. “The first of them is around security. It’s very hard to securely provide access to AI agents, and that’s one of the top challenges.”

Özbütün spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at Oracle AI World, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI architecture and the challenges of moving agents into production. (* Disclosure below.)

Security is the first hurdle. AI agents are finding vulnerabilities at unprecedented levels, and customers often can’t patch their databases before attackers exploit those flaws, Özbütün noted. Oracle’s Autonomous AI Database encrypts data at rest and in transit by default, and users can’t turn those protections off.

“As soon as the vulnerability is found, before it’s released anywhere else, we bring it into production in Autonomous AI Database,” Özbütün said.

Resiliency is the next test, because agents run around the clock and put heavy, unpredictable demands on the data platform. Oracle commits to 99.995% availability with no exclusions. That figure is measured by whether a client can connect and run queries, not by whether the underlying infrastructure is running, Özbütün explained.

“We patch our systems on a weekly basis, for example,” Özbütün said. “All of our patches are online patches, so the database is up and running, accepting new connections, accepting new requests while we’re running the patch.”

The same always-current approach applies to Oracle’s Deep Trust AI architecture, in which the database enforces the security profiles that customers define. New capabilities such as the expanded Deep Data Security features show up in Autonomous AI Database as soon as they’re announced, ahead of on-premises releases, according to Özbütün.

“You do nothing as the user or administrator of Autonomous Database to get this functionality,” Özbütün said. “As soon as a new functionality is available, like Oracle Deep Data Security, it becomes available for you to use on day one.”

#5553. Secure borders. A stronger economy. Washington must deliver both

The editorial calls for immigration enforcement that protects due process and lawful work, plus modernized pathways aligned to construction labor needs. It points to Harvard and NAHB data and urges homebuilding leaders to press for measurable policy outcomes on affordability and productivity.  AI Summary

In the first 100 days of the Trump administration, business leaders at residential construction and development companies were, in effect, summoned to the nation’s capital for an all-hands meeting with administration officials on housing affordability. The summons came on short notice, on a Sunday afternoon. The invitation carried an undertone. Attend or else.

The Washington, D.C., meeting never took place. But the episode captured the breakneck pace and take-no-prisoners approach of those early, flood-the-zone months. It also dialed in a distinctly unsettling tone for the rules of engagement between the new administration and the nation’s private-sector business leaders in one of the economy’s critical engines: homebuilding.

Now, following the 2026 midterm elections, those rules of engagement stand an opportunity to change.

Business leaders, including corporate strategists and their representatives on Capitol Hill, have a window to act quickly, elevate their priorities, and press for policy changes that have damaged or threaten to undermine some of the nation’s most important economic capabilities.

For homebuilding, residential development, and residential investment, immigration enforcement belongs near the top of the agenda.

The United States needs secure borders and enforceable immigration laws. It also needs the workforce capacity to build homes, grow food, manufacture products, and sustain economic growth. These are not competing national interests, and treating them as such has real economic consequences.

The question for President Trump, the incoming Congress, and the business leaders with a stake in the outcome is whether the next two years can achieve a more rational, workable balance among those objectives.

For the housing industry, evidence of what’s at risk is already accumulating.

Over recent months, HousingWire TBD has documented the increasingly disruptive effects of immigration enforcement on residential construction businesses and their trade partners.

Builders and contractors report job site interruptions, workers reluctant to report for work, and crews disappearing from construction schedules. In some affected markets, executives have reported reductions of 60% to 80% in available trade crews. These are accounts from specific businesses and markets, not nationwide estimates.

The disruption also extends beyond workers who lack legal authorization. Reports that U.S. citizens and legally authorized workers are apprehensive about reporting to job sites suggest that enforcement-related fear can diminish workforce availability and productivity.

Residential construction depends on the coordinated sequencing of specialized trades. When a framing crew is unavailable, subsequent work may be delayed, schedules are extended, financing costs accumulate, and closings slip.

For builders and their trade partners operating with already compressed margins and limited capital flexibility, repeated disruptions can pose a serious business risk.

These accounts do not establish that immigration enforcement has caused a nationwide construction crisis. They do, however, raise a question policymakers cannot responsibly ignore: Are enforcement practices achieving legitimate security objectives while imposing avoidable economic costs on lawful workers, responsible employers, and American households?

A study published on October 8 by Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies found that foreign-born workers accounted for 35% of the nation’s construction trades workforce in 2024, compared with 18% of the overall U.S. labor force.

Their representation is especially high in trades critical to home completion: 57% of drywall and ceiling-tile installers, 53% of roofers and painters, and 51% of flooring installers were foreign-born.

Harvard’s research found that foreign-born workers accounted for all net growth in the construction trades workforce from 2013 to 2024.

Separate NAHB research found that Hispanic workers represented 32.8% of the construction workforce in 2024, up from 23.6% in 2010. In Texas and California, approximately six in 10 construction workers are Hispanic.

Foreign-born status, Hispanic ethnicity, citizenship, and legal employment authorization are distinct characteristics. These statistics cannot be used interchangeably to describe immigration status. Nor do they, nor can they, truly reflect the full impact of foreign-born workers on job site capability and productivity because many undocumented frontline crew members are not counted at all.

The statistics, however, illustrate the industry’s substantial dependence on a diverse workforce, whose lawful participation must be protected.

Meanwhile, labor shortages are worsening despite reduced housing production. NAHB’s September 2026 survey found that, averaged across nine consistently tracked trades, 47% of builders reported labor shortages, up from 42% in April 2025. Framing shortages reached 57%, while finished carpentry shortages reached 58%.

NAHB also identified immigration-enforcement-related worker apprehensions as a contributor to worsening shortages, along with competition from other construction sectors.

Immigration enforcement did not create the industry’s longstanding workforce problems. Those problems reflect decades of insufficient domestic workforce development, shifting demographics, competition for skilled labor, and limited productivity gains. But making an already constrained workforce even less available cannot be a rational part of a national housing affordability strategy.

Washington does not need to start from scratch.

Bipartisan immigration reform initiatives have repeatedly recognized the need to combine effective border security, lawful employment pathways, immigration-system modernization, and solutions for established workers and employers.

NAHB’s comprehensive immigration reform policy, updated in November 2025, provides a practical foundation for the industry. It supports border security and effective enforcement, along with construction-specific visa reforms, legal workforce pathways, and domestic workforce development.

The association has also endorsed the bipartisan DIGNITY Act, which would strengthen border security while establishing conditional pathways to lawful employment for certain undocumented workers who meet defined requirements.

These proposals involve difficult choices and legitimate disagreements. They show that practical approaches exist beyond the familiar binary choice between unrestricted enforcement and abandoning enforcement altogether.

The remaining weeks of the current Congress and the next two years should be evaluated against three governing objectives.

First, the administration must enforce immigration laws while protecting lawful employment and upholding due process. Enforcement priorities, worker-identification procedures, and accountability mechanisms should minimize unnecessary disruption to legitimate businesses and protect citizens and authorized workers from improper detention or interference.

Second, Congress and the administration must develop lawful workforce pathways that reflect documented economic needs. That means considering construction-specific employment programs, modernizing immigration processing, and addressing established workers’ circumstances through clear eligibility, screening, compliance, and worker-protection requirements.

Third, immigration policymaking must elevate economic productivity and affordability as measurable priorities. Congress should assess workforce availability, construction delays, business costs and housing production alongside border-security and enforcement outcomes.

None of these objectives diminishes employers’ obligation to comply with the law, protect workers, invest in apprenticeships and technical education, or to improve productivity through innovation.

America needs stronger domestic workforce development and a workable immigration policy, not one in place of the other.

The industry’s responsibility cannot end with documenting the disruption and asking Washington for relief. Homebuilders, residential developers, investors, building-products manufacturers, trade contractors, and their associations have the evidence, economic standing, and organizational capacity to demand a coherent policy response.

NAHB has already established a reform framework and identified legislative priorities. Industry executives have documented the operational consequences, and research institutions have quantified the workforce’s dependence on immigration.

What, then, are business leaders waiting for?

The next step should be a coordinated, industry-wide agenda presented to the administration and congressional leadership, including specific legislative priorities, credible evidence of business impacts, and commitments to lawful employment, investment in the domestic workforce, and improved productivity.

Not another statement of concern. Not another round of partisan accusations. A sustained effort to translate widely acknowledged economic needs into workable policy.

The new political balance in Washington creates an opening, but divided government does not automatically lead to better governance. Progress will require leaders willing to negotiate, make difficult choices, and accept accountability for results.

The homebuilding industry should not passively wait to see whether that happens. Its leaders have both a direct business interest and a broader responsibility to help make it possible.

America should not have to choose between secure borders and a productive economy. President Trump and Congress should be held accountable for delivering on both fronts.

Not only should the homebuilding industry insist that it do so, but the industry’s leaders should strike with the same speed and ferocity the Administration used to kick-start its agenda almost two years ago.

#5551. Block DOJ Settlement: Jack Dorsey’s Company Faces $764M Deal as Bitcoin Profit Plunges 50%

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Block DOJ settlement talks have reached a major turning point, with Jack Dorsey-owned payments company agreeing in principle to pay $764 million. The proposed deal would resolve a federal investigation into alleged failures in its anti-money laundering controls.

The agreement follows years of scrutiny over Block’s Cash App compliance practices. The company disclosed the development in its quarterly filing yesterday, outlining a deferred prosecution agreement with the U.S. Department of Justice.

Jack Dorsey’s Block has beaten Q3 earnings estimates, posting $3.2B in gross profit.The company has also raised its 2026 outlook, while warning that a potential DOJ settlement could be larger than expected.Strong results and a higher forecast from one of the biggest names in… pic.twitter.com/Bk0KByUDPV

The announcement arrives alongside a sharp decline in Block’s Bitcoin business. Bitcoin ecosystem gross profit plunged 50% year-over-year to $52 million during the third quarter, despite stronger overall company earnings.

The proposed Block DOJ agreement would defer prosecution for three years over allegations that the company failed to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program. The DOJ’s investigation centers on compliance requirements under the Bank Secrecy Act. Block would need to meet obligations outlined in the agreement throughout its term.

If the company fully complies, prosecutors would move to dismiss the deferred charges. However, the resolution remains subject to final agreement terms and court approval.

The proposed settlement carries a gross monetary component of approximately $964 million. Credits for previous regulatory resolutions would reduce the expected net payment to roughly $764 million. Block has already accrued $764 million for the matter as of September 30. The company warned that the final cost could exceed that amount.

The investigation dates back to 2023, when federal authorities began examining Block’s compliance practices and related disclosures. The scrutiny followed allegations raised by short seller Hindenburg Research.

Block rejected those allegations as inaccurate and misleading. Separately, New York’s financial regulator fined the company $40 million in 2025 over compliance failures.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The Block DOJ development comes as the company’s Bitcoin business faces a sharp profitability decline. Block reported Bitcoin ecosystem gross profit of $52 million in Q3, down from $104 million a year earlier. The company attributed the decline primarily to lower fees on certain Bitcoin transactions through Cash App.

Bitcoin-related revenue reached approximately $1.8 billion during the quarter. However, the lower fees significantly reduced the amount Block retained from its Bitcoin operations.

The weakness contrasts with stronger performance across the broader business. Block reported $3.24 billion in total gross profit, up 22% year-over-year. Cash App gross profit climbed 27% to $2.07 billion. Square gross profit increased 14%, while quarterly net income rose to approximately $566 million.

Block also raised its full-year 2026 gross profit forecast to $12.63 billion, representing expected growth of roughly 22%.

Now, proposed Block DOJ settlement creates a major legal expense alongside a mixed earnings picture. Its Bitcoin business is generating less profit, even as Cash App and Square support stronger company-wide growth.

#5550. University of Utah retains operational sovereignty as Redtail expands research access

Operational sovereignty gives universities authority over how shared computing resources are allocated, managed and secured.

The University of Utah’s Redtail AI factory supercomputer brings advanced computing capabilities to a statewide community. Supporting researchers, students, administrators and external partners through that infrastructure requires more than computing capacity, according to Manish Parashar (pictured), chief AI officer of the University of Utah.

“In research, we are always trying to balance research security with doing open research for societal good,” he said. “Depending on where you are, you might want to lean in one direction or the other. Having that capability to turn the knob becomes so important.”

Parashar spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin for the “Sovereign AI: From Strategy to Reality” video series, during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed university control of computing infrastructure, research governance and the investment needed to support Utah’s expanding ambitions. (* Disclosure below.)

Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. helped architect and deploy Redtail as a turnkey system. The university’s Center for High Performance Computing operates it, drawing on expertise that also supports separate regulated research environments, Parashar explained.

“They have admin access, they’re doing the allocations, they are doing the onboarding,” he said. “They’re doing the management and monitoring … the optimization [and] … the right sizing.”

The interview examined Utah’s approach through theCUBE Research’s Five Pillars of Sovereign AI framework: Territorial, Legal, Technological, Operational and Financial. The university retains operational and legal responsibilities, while financing rests on partnerships with the state and donors, according to Parashar.

“Our overall ecosystem is a hybrid,” he said. “There’s things that are on-prem, there are things that are cloud-hosted, and we always will look at it as a hybrid system. Not everything has to be territorially in a single data center or in the state.”

Redtail also gives the university a way to accommodate growing demand for protected computing by freeing up capacity in existing facilities. Current environments support sensitive and regulated research, including healthcare projects, and expanding their capacity is a priority, Parashar noted.

“How do we move into a facility that has not only the capacity, but is also compliant with emerging controls that are coming out? We want to grow that out, and that’s our focus right now,” he said. “And what happens is with the Redtail, a lot of our open research moves to that and that frees up capacity in our data center and other places where we can grow out this regulated environment.”

The university’s One-U Responsible AI initiative connects research with broader societal needs. Its work spans innovation, public-sector collaboration and regional challenges such as air quality, Parashar explained.

“Being open there becomes very, very important because you want to bring the best ideas, the best data — and most often, it is citizen data that’s coming in — and be able to then see how we can most effectively use AI to address this very regional challenge,” he said. “We don’t want to lose ideas; we don’t want to lose the data that’s coming in. We want to assimilate it and make sure the outcome and the warnings that come out of that — the notifications — are as broadly disseminated as possible.”

Financial sustainability must accommodate rising demand as well as technology refreshes. Expansion planning began before the Redtail contract was signed, and the university is approaching federal agencies, including the Department of Energy and the National Science Foundation, about investing in the existing ecosystem, Parashar noted.

“We are talking to the state and showing them value — very quickly — and convincing them that investing in this is good for the state [and] it’s good for its citizens,” he said. “We are [also] talking to additional philanthropic donors.”

The university’s statewide mission extends beyond providing access to computing resources. Training, workforce development and shared expertise are also part of the ecosystem that operational sovereignty must support, according to Parashar.

“It’s not that we need everything to be tightly controlled. We don’t want everything to be completely open,” he said. “We want to make sure we have the ability to right-size it depending on what we are working on.”

#5549. The 8 habits the American Heart Association says to protect your heart

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The American Heart Association's Life's Essential 8 covers diet, activity, tobacco, sleep, weight, cholesterol, blood sugar, and blood pressure.

A typical day holds many small choices about what to eat, how far to walk, and when to turn off the lights. Few of those choices register as medical decisions, yet together they shape the condition of the heart and blood vessels over years. Stronger cardiovascular health cuts the odds of heart disease and stroke, along with other serious illnesses. The payoff extends beyond one organ. Everyday routines amount to a long-running health plan, whether or not anyone writes it down. A clear checklist turns that plan into something a person can follow, revisit, and adjust.

Cardiovascular needs shift across a lifetime, and women meet several turning points along the way. Pregnancy, motherhood, and menopause can each raise a woman's chances of heart disease and stroke. A woman's heart health can also reach the next generation. A mother's cardiovascular well-being shapes her baby's for years after birth. Good heart health begins before a child arrives. The checklist reflects those life stages with separate versions for women, for pregnancy, and for kids. People who want a sense of where they stand can turn to My Life Check, a self-assessment tool that produces a heart health score. The tool offers a baseline, and the checklist supplies the habits to improve on.

American Heart Association guidance presents Life's Essential 8 as the organization's core measures for building and sustaining cardiovascular health. The eight measures fall into two broad areas, Health Behaviors and Health Factors, though the group does not say which item belongs where. The association's web page reports no study, survey, sample, or rating formula, and it does not explain how My Life Check calculates its results. The page works as a consumer guide, and the association says it reviewed and approved all health information on its site, drawing on scientific research and its own guidelines. Every measure carries a short description, and each links to a downloadable fact sheet offered in other languages as well. The numbering below follows the association's list order and implies no hierarchy of importance. This article covers all eight measures in that sequence.

Eat Better opens the American Heart Association's list of eight measures with a call for an overall healthy eating pattern built on whole foods, plenty of fruits and vegetables, lean protein, nuts, and seeds. The guidance also steers cooking toward non-tropical oils, naming olive and canola as examples. A downloadable fact sheet and a "Learn how to" link round out the entry, which sets no numeric target.

The entry reads more like a shopping list than a formula. It names categories of food and leaves portions, calories, and serving counts unstated. Whole foods lead the description, and fruits and vegetables draw the only hint of quantity, with the page asking for lots of them. Protein comes with one qualifier, lean, which narrows the choice without ruling out any source. Nuts and seeds fill out the foods. The oil guidance sorts by type, setting two named options against a tropical category the page never spells out.

Framing the measure as a pattern points it at diet across many meals. One salad or one heavy dinner counts for little against what a person eats week after week, and the sustained habit is what the checklist asks for.

Healthy Eating heads the site's list of related resource topics, ahead of Fitness, Quit Nicotine, Sleep, Losing Weight, Cholesterol, Diabetes, and Blood Pressure. Those topics track the numbered measures one for one. A reader who starts with food can follow the same order through the rest of the association's material.

Four other entries supply a benchmark a reader can test against, covering weekly activity minutes, nightly sleep hours, body mass index, and a blood pressure reading. Eat Better offers no comparable yardstick on the checklist. Progress on diet comes down to how closely meals match the foods the entry names, with the fact sheet and the Healthy Eating resources available for specifics.

To be more active, the American Heart Association asks adults to log 2½ hours of moderate physical activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity each week. Both routes satisfy the same requirement, and the gap between them reveals how the guidance weighs effort. Two and a half hours equals 150 minutes, so the vigorous option demands half the time on the clock. In effect, the AHA counts one minute of hard exertion as worth two at a moderate pace.

A weekly target leaves adults room to arrange their own schedules. Spread across seven days, the moderate goal works out to about 21 minutes a day, and the vigorous goal comes to about 11. A busy Tuesday does not sink the plan. The AHA tallies the total across the full week, so someone with a crowded workweek can shift more of the minutes to days with open time.

Children answer to a stricter standard, with the AHA calling for 60 minutes of activity every day. Across a week, those daily sessions add up to 420 minutes, 2.8 times the adult moderate benchmark. The adult moderate goal, averaged out, fills about a third of a child's daily hour. A daily mandate removes the calendar slack adults enjoy. A child cannot bank extra time on Saturday to cover a quiet Monday. Play earns credit toward the hour alongside structured activities, which broadens the menu and puts a child's free time to work for the heart.

Partial progress toward these numbers has value of its own. Any amount of movement outperforms none, and adults coming off an inactive stretch should build up their activity in stages. A beginner can start with a few moderate minutes and add more each week. Every increment counts toward the weekly total, so the climb itself delivers part of the payoff.

Traditional cigarette smoking drives most preventable deaths, the checklist warns. Newer nicotine products have joined the field. E-cigarettes and vaping arrived later, and researchers have yet to finish measuring what long-term use does to the body. The open question around vaping leaves the cigarette as the product with the clearest and most lethal record.

About 40% of U.S. children ages 3 to 11 breathe secondhand smoke, which spreads the danger to people who never lit anything. The figure stretches from preschoolers to kids finishing elementary school. None of them chose to inhale those fumes. Exposure on that scale makes tobacco a household issue as much as a personal one. A parent or caregiver who quits removes one source of that exposure from a child's daily surroundings.

Quitting rewards the heart on a short timeline. The steepest drop in coronary heart disease risk comes in the first one to two years after a person stops, with a gentler slide in later years, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Giving up cigarettes reduces markers of inflammation and of the blood's tendency to clot, and it lifts HDL cholesterol in quick order. Stroke odds shrink in parallel, approaching the level seen in people who never smoked. Former smokers face a smaller chance of an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and the gap widens the longer a person stays smoke-free. Researchers can chart how cigarette damage recedes across years without tobacco. E-cigarettes have not yet built up a comparable body of evidence.

Age and smoking history leave the benefit intact. Long-term and heavy smokers gain from stopping, and the payoff holds at any stage of life. People living with coronary heart disease can lower their chances of another heart attack and of dying from heart disease once they quit. Quitting doubles as protection for hearts that coronary disease has damaged.

Most adults need seven to nine hours of sleep every night, a window the American Heart Association writes into its eight-part checklist for heart health. Checking the target takes no lab work. A bedtime and a wake-up time supply the whole calculation.

Children require more rest, and the amount shrinks as they grow. Kids age 5 and younger need 10 to 16 hours, and the guidance folds naps into the total for this group alone. Children ages 6 to 12 should get nine to 12 hours, and teens ages 13 to 18 need eight to 10 hours. At its upper end, the youngest group's range fills two-thirds of a 24-hour day. The oldest group's floor sits an hour above the adult minimum. A 16-year-old who sleeps seven hours, an amount that satisfies an adult, falls below the teen range.

The spread between minimum and maximum also tightens with age. The span for the youngest children covers six hours, the span for school-age kids covers three, and teens and adults each get a two-hour band. Ten hours marks both the floor for the youngest group and the ceiling for teens. School-age children can need as many as three hours more than the adult maximum.

Adequate sleep helps the body heal, sharpens brain function, and lowers the risk of chronic disease, according to the association. Research ties insufficient sleep to higher odds of obesity, diabetes, and high blood pressure. Each of those conditions raises the likelihood of heart disease. Short nights, repeated over time, can feed the problem the checklist exists to prevent.

Obesity, diabetes, and high blood pressure correspond to three other entries on the same list, which gives weight, blood sugar, and blood pressure their own lines. Researchers said scientists have yet to pin down how poor sleep leads to heart disease. They added that better sleep could benefit the heart. A full night of rest may serve several measures on the checklist at once.

A body mass index under 25 marks the optimal weight on the checklist, turning a fuzzy goal into a number anyone can follow. BMI expresses a person's weight relative to height as a single figure, and the American Heart Association treats it as a helpful yardstick. Height enters the calculation, so two people who weigh the same can land on opposite sides of 25. The index has a floor. A reading below 18.5 counts as underweight. The two thresholds frame an optimal band 6.5 points wide, opening at 18.5 and closing short of 25.

Trouble can come from either direction. The underweight line keeps the goal from turning into a race toward the smallest possible number. Reaching a healthy weight and holding it there brings many benefits, according to the association. A single good reading falls short of the measure, which asks people to stay inside those limits over time.

Excess body fat travels with an unhealthy lipid profile. Obesity, the term for that excess, tracks with higher levels of "bad" cholesterol and triglycerides and lower levels of "good" cholesterol. The same condition can help bring on high blood pressure, diabetes, and heart disease. Cholesterol and blood pressure each hold a separate slot among the eight, which places weight beside two other items that obesity touches. A person whose weight climbs may see the effects surface on more than one line of the checklist.

An online calculator or a health care professional can supply a personal BMI, the association notes. Either route rests on two inputs, height and weight, which makes the result easy to recheck as habits change. Repeated checks can show whether a person is drifting toward the 25 line before crossing it. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that people with obesity work with their medical team on a plan to lower their weight.

High levels of non-HDL cholesterol, the type the American Heart Association calls "bad," can lead to heart disease. The warning steers attention toward one slice of the blood's cholesterol and away from the overall total.

The non-HDL count comes from taking total cholesterol and subtracting the HDL portion. The remainder holds LDL along with other types such as VLDL. LDL carries its "bad" reputation as the leading cause of the cholesterol buildup that clogs arteries. HDL earns a "good" label by helping clear cholesterol out of those vessels. Stripping out the helpful fraction leaves a figure built around the main culprit behind blocked arteries. A total reading, by contrast, folds protective and harmful cholesterol into one number. A high total can include a generous share of HDL.

A health care professional may treat non-HDL cholesterol as a better number to follow than total cholesterol, according to the association. The group gives two reasons. Patients need not fast before the test, and the calculation yields a dependable result for everyone. The usual preparation for a lipid panel, the blood test that measures cholesterol, allows nothing but water ahead of the draw. The no-fasting option removes one hurdle between a person and a cholesterol screening. A test that skips the fast and works for any patient also suits repeat checks, letting someone see whether changes in diet, activity, or smoking show up in the number.

Cutting high cholesterol can start with a diet light on saturated fat, regular exercise, and an end to smoking. Doctors can add prescription drugs such as statins. All three habits mirror other measures on the same list: Eat Better, Be More Active, and Quit Tobacco. Progress on any of those fronts can help pull non-HDL levels down as well. A person working through the list in order meets the cholesterol item after three habits that feed into it.

Blood sugar that stays high for a long stretch can damage four parts of the body: the heart, the kidneys, the eyes, and the nerves. The kidneys, eyes, and nerves sit outside the cardiovascular system, so the stakes of this measure reach past heart disease.

Glucose starts at the dinner table. The body breaks most of what a person eats down into this blood-borne sugar and then burns it for energy.

The body depends on this sugar as fuel, which locates the danger in levels that remain elevated over time.

PIPELINE-SHORTFALL: Slide 7 — This slide runs about 90 words, short of the 300-word minimum. The supplied notes for Manage Blood Sugar cover how the body turns food into glucose for energy and how sustained high blood sugar can harm the heart, kidneys, eyes, and nerves, and they do not supply enough further substance to reach the minimum. No approved supplementary details cover this measure. The slide states only what that evidence supports.

The American Heart Association treats blood pressure readings below 120/80 mm Hg as optimal, and it offers no other threshold for this measure. Keeping pressure inside healthy ranges, the AHA notes, can lengthen the years a person stays well. The group steers readers to a separate summary of 10 key facts from its high blood pressure guideline. Each reading measures a physical force. Blood pressure tracks how hard blood pushes against the walls of the arteries with each heartbeat. A reading qualifies as high once that force stays elevated over time.

Hypertension, the medical term for high blood pressure, tends to produce no signs or symptoms anyone would notice. People can feel fine while their pressure runs high. A measurement provides the sole way to learn whether pressure has climbed. Readings rise and fall over the course of a day. A health care provider may take several of them across more than one visit before diagnosing high blood pressure. Clinicians may suggest home checks with a validated monitor to help confirm the result. One high number at a single appointment may not settle the matter. The AHA's target means little without a reading to hold against it.

Everyday habits and medication that a patient takes as prescribed can bring high blood pressure under control. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suggests going over several lifestyle steps with a health care team. Its recommendations cover regular physical activity, avoiding tobacco, a healthy diet that limits sodium and alcohol, a healthy weight, and stress management. Four of those steps line up with separate measures on the AHA's list: activity, tobacco, diet, and weight. Bringing pressure down can cut the risk of heart disease and stroke, which share the label cardiovascular disease. One blood pressure reading can capture progress across four other measures on the checklist.

#5548. NYC pied-a-terre tax notices get an appeals court green light

A state appeals court dismissed a homeowners’ lawsuit that had disrupted NYC’s pied-a-terre tax notice rollout, finding no standing or injury. A separate challenge by Steve Wynn and Wilbur Ross to the underlying state law remains pending.  AI Summary

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration won another round on the pied-à-terre tax Wednesday, when a state appeals court dismissed a homeowners’ lawsuit that had upended the surcharge’s rollout.

Appeals judges threw out an earlier Staten Island judge’s ruling ordering the city to cancel about 17,000 notices. They found the homeowners lacked standing and weren’t injured by the notices. All four judges agreed.

The surcharge is a pillar in the city’s plan to close a $12 billion budget gap. State officials projected it would raise about $500 million a year. The comptroller estimates the impact at closer to $1 billion before exemptions and appeals.

Wednesday’s decision does not directly affect a separate suit by billionaire casino magnate Steve Wynn, former Trump administration Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross and his wife. They have challenged the state law behind the tax. That case remains pending in Suffolk County, with hearings scheduled in December.

A Staten Island judge had ruled Sept. 29 that the city skipped individualized decisions before mailing notices. The judge called the notices arbitrary and capricious and a due process violation.

Under the order, the Department of Finance was to cancel the notices and pull its roll from the agency website. New notices were allowed after an individualized review. Within hours, the city appealed and invoked a stay, so implementation continued.

Residential brokers told HousingWire TBD that the legal back-and-forth and the tax itself have had little impact on the owner-occupied market.

Ian Slater, co-founder and CEO of Trove Partners, said the market for under $5 million slowed in September and October. “We hit a record number of contract signatures above $5 million in September and October,” he said.

Wealth from a soaring stock market, plus nerves about its froth, is pushing buyers into top-end property, Slater said. Those buyers are “fully ignoring the pied-à-terre tax.” Some want second homes in New York City, he said.

However, listings of such properties remain scarce. Jessica Chestler, co-founder of The Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman, said bidding wars have erupted. Supply isn’t keeping pace with buyer demand, including for homes priced above $5 million.

“We recently represented a buyer in a bidding war that we ultimately won, but it required going $1 million over asking on an apartment that needed a complete gut renovation,” Chestler said.

Because the homeowners lacked standing, the court never ruled on whether the NYC Department of Finance’s rollout was lawful. The court said other arguments were either without merit or unnecessary to resolve.

Finance later used 2025 tax data to revise its determinations, the court noted. Several hundred owners learned they did not owe the surcharge. The surcharge covers only non-primary residences. Through July 2028, the measure impacts houses worth $5 million or more. Co-ops and condos face a $1 million threshold.

Wynn and the Rosses sued in late September. They argue the surcharge is an illegal property tax that discriminates against nonresidents. Wynn’s notice totaled $183,094.69, while the Rosses’ notice came to $83,531.52.

Trove Partners’ Slater does not expect the climate to change. “Political winds are clearly against the wealthy class,” he said.

He doubts judges or politicians will move away from the tax. “It’s definitely an annoyance, but it’s a bit of much ado about nothing,” he said.
